stem: A 29-year-old woman who has vitamin D-resistant rickets comes to the genetics clinic with her partner as they want to discuss starting a family. She is worried about how her children will be affected by the disease. Which of the following fits best with the clinical picture?
options: All female children will be free of symptoms
All male children will be free of symptoms
Half of female children will have worse symptoms than their mother
All male children will have worse symptoms than their mother
None of their children will inherit the disease
explanation:
All male children will have worse symptoms than their mother
This is because vitamin D-resistant rickets is an X-linked dominant disorder. This means that symptoms occur in both women and men, but because women carry two X chromosomes, symptoms are generally less severe in women.

All female children will be free of symptoms
All female children will be free of symptoms is incorrect as this is an X-linked dominant disorder, meaning that although women will have symptoms, these are generally less severe versus men.

All male children will be free of symptoms
All male children will be free of symptoms is incorrect as in X-linked recessive disorders men suffer a greater symptomatic burden than women.

Half of female children will have worse symptoms than their mother
Half of female children will have worse symptoms than their mother is incorrect as in the event that they inherit the abnormal chromosome from their mother, symptoms will be the same. Osteomalacia and RicketsNone of their children will inherit the disease
None of their children will inherit the disease is incorrect as any children have a 50% chance of inheriting the abnormal gene from their mother.

stem: You are asked to see a family with suspected Huntington's disease for genetic counselling. The family has come across the term 'genetic anticipation' on the internet. Which of the following best corresponds to the definition of this term?
options: Selected symptoms of the disease occur before others
Symptoms of the disease are more severe at onset but then resolve over time
Symptoms of the disease occur at a progressively younger age with each generation
Symptoms of the disease occur only in children
Symptoms of the disease skip a generation
explanation:
Symptoms of the disease occur at a progressively younger age with each generation
Genetic anticipation is seen in inherited neurological disorders. It occurs because of expansion of trinucleotide repeat sequences across successive generations. Huntington’s disease, myotonic dystrophy and spinal cerebellar ataxias are examples of diseases where genetic anticipation is seen.

Selected symptoms of the disease occur before others
Selected symptoms of the disease occur before others is incorrect. Selected symptoms of the disease occur before others is incorrect as this is seen in some mitochondrial disorders such as DIDMOAD syndrome, where symptoms often appear progressively: one disorder, such as diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus or deafness, appears to manifest before the others in the syndrome.

Symptoms of the disease are more severe at onset but then resolve over time
Symptoms of the disease are more severe at onset but then resolve over time is incorrect. Symptoms of the disease are more severe at onset but then resolve over time is incorrect as Huntington’s disease progresses overtime.

Symptoms of the disease occur only in children
Symptoms of the disease occur only in children is incorrect. Symptoms of the disease occur only in children is incorrect as this tends to be the pattern in inherited disorders with high lethality, where death occurs in childhood. Huntington’s DiseaseSymptoms of the disease skip a generation
Symptoms of the disease skip a generation is incorrect. Symptoms of the disease skip a generation is incorrect as diseases which appear to skip a generation because only mild symptoms, or none at all, are seen, are said to display incomplete penetrance.

stem: A 47-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with a history of recurrent abdominal pain and recent episodes of rectal bleeding. On examination, she has multiple pigmented macules on her lips and oral mucosa. Her mother had a similar pigmentation pattern and was diagnosed with intestinal polyps. What is the most likely pattern of inheritance for her condition?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
Peutz-Jeghers syndrome (PJS) is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder characterized by the development of hamartomatous polyps in the GI tract and mucocutaneous pigmentation, such as pigmented macules on the lips, oral mucosa, and other areas. The condition results from mutations in the STK11 gene (also known as LKB1). The inheritance pattern means that only one copy of the mutated gene is required to manifest symptoms; hence it often appears in successive generations without skipping.

Autosomal recessive
For an autosomal recessive disorder to present clinically, both copies of a gene must be mutated. This would typically mean that neither parent may show symptoms if they are carriers unless both contribute a defective allele. Given that Peutz-Jeghers syndrome follows an autosomal dominant pattern where only one altered gene from either parent can cause disease manifestation, this option does not apply.

Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial inheritance involves genes transmitted exclusively through maternal lineage via mitochondrial DNA affecting all offspring regardless of sex but not following Mendelian patterns seen with nuclear DNA disorders. PJS involves mutations in nuclear DNA specifically inherited in an autosomal fashion Chatrather with AIthan Tutor maternally through mitochondria.

X-linked dominant
An X-linked dominant disorder would affect both sexes if they have just one copy of a mutated allele but shows different expressivity due to gender differences related to X chromosome dosage compensation mechanisms like Lyonisation or X-inactivation (In females, although each body cell has two X chromosomes, only one is used for making the gene product and the other X chromosome is inactivated). PJS does not follow this mode as its genetic basis lies within autosomes rather than sex chromosomes.

X-linked recessive
Conditions following this inheritance mode predominantly affect men because they possess only one X chromosome which, when carrying a mutation without another normal counterpart (as seen with women who have two), leads directly to phenotype expression. Since Peutz-Jeghers syndrome affects men and women equally based on its location within non-sex-determined chromosomes (autosomes), this option is incorrect. Peutz-Jeghers.

stem: A female patient with a history of xeroderma pigmentosum comes to the dermatology clinic for review. Her underlying condition is thought to be at least in part related to a defect in DNA repair, replication and transcription. Which of the following enzymes separates strands of DNA in replication?
explanation:
Helicase
Helicase plays a role in DNA repair, replication and transcription; they are motor proteins that move directionally along a nucleic acid phosphodiester backbone, separating two annealed nucleic acid strands.

Nuclease
Nuclease is incorrect. The primary function of nucleases is to remove a sequence of DNA which aids the DNA repair process and can, indirectly contribute to replicationn.

Phosphodiesterase
Phosphodiesterase is incorrect. Phosphodiesterases break down phosphodiesterase bonds. They are primarily a target for pharmacological inhibition in the treatment of a diverse range of conditions, including erectile dysfunction and asthma.

Restriction endonuclease
Restriction endonuclease is incorrect. These are a subset of nucleases that cut DNA molecules at a limited number of specific nucleotide sequences.

Telomerase
Telomerase is incorrect. These are responsible for telomere repair to prevent progressive shortening during replication.

stem: A 30-year-old man presents to the endocrinology clinic for review. He has problems in his relationship, and has looked for treatments for erectile dysfunction. On examination his BP is 115/70 mmHg; pulse is 67 bpm and regular. He is 1.94 m tall. You note gynaecomastia and bilateral small testes. He tells you he tried to enrol as a sperm donor some years ago but was refused due to a low sperm count. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Klinefelter syndrome
The combination of tall stature, gynaecomastia and infertility due to azoospermia is diagnostic. Almost all men with Klinefelter syndrome are azoospermic. Other features of this condition include: Reduced facial hair Tendency to obesity Small atrophic testes. Mild learning difficulties can be seen in some patients with Klinefelter syndrome, but intellectual disability is not a feature of this condition. Chromosome analysis will show 47 chromosomes, with two X and one Y chromosome (47, XXY)

Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is incorrect as although it does result in azoospermia, the other features, including tall stature and gynaecomastia, are not present.

Homocystinuria
Homocystinuria is incorrect as although these patients have tall stature, learning difficulties, lens dislocation, osteoporosis and recurrent arterial thrombosis, they do not suffer from azoospermia or gynaecomastia.

Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome is incorrect as this is associated with tall stature, lens and joint dislocation, but not reduced sexual function. Klinefelter SyndromeAn 18-year-old army recruit undergoes preliminary health screening and is found to have a Hb of 115 g/l (NR 130–170). Spherocytes are present in the peripheral blood film. Investigation of his siblings reveals that one of his two brothers also has spherocytic anaemia and had his gallbladder removed. In which one of the following is a defect most frequently responsible for this condition?

XYY syndrome
XYY syndrome is incorrect as this is associated with tall stature but not gynaecomastia or azoospermia.

stem: You are asked to review a young man with short stature, short 5 th metacarpals, subcutaneous calcification, intellectual impairment and hypocalcaemia. Given the likely clinical diagnosis, where is the most likely defect?
options: A G-protein linked to the parathyroid hormone (PTH) receptor
An ion channel linked to the PTH receptor
explanation:
A G-protein linked to the parathyroid hormone (PTH) receptor
This man has pseudohypoparathyroidism, related to a loss-of-function mutation affecting the G-protein-linked receptor for PTH. When the G-protein-linked receptor is activated by a ligand it binds a trimeric complex (alpha, beta and gamma), which is anchored to the inner surface of the plasma membrane. This trimeric complex is called a guanosine triphosphate (GTP)-binding protein, or G-protein. The G-protein receptor then binds GTP and interacts with enzymes on the inner membrane surface to activate one of a number of secondary messengers, which may include: Cyclic adenosine monophosphate (AMP) Calcium ions Inositol 1,4,5-trisphosphate or diacylglycerol There may also be variable degrees of resistance to other G-protein-linked hormones apart from PTH, including thyroid-stimulating hormone, luteinising hormone and follicle-stimulating hormone.

A serine kinase receptor
A serine kinase receptor is incorrect as these mutations play a role in cell proliferation disorders, an example being the BRAF mutation.

A tyrosine kinase receptor
A tyrosine kinase receptor mutation is incorrect as these mutations have an important role in the development of haematological cancers.

A tyrosine phosphatase receptor
A tyrosine phosphatase receptor is incorrect as these mutations are associated with the development of head and neck cancers via the STAT3 mutation. He also described a feeling of impending doom during these episodes, in addition to severe headache and dizziness. He had no other medical history. He stated that his father had had a problem with his pancreas, and had died of metastatic cancer. On examination his blood pressure was 176/98 mmHg standing and 132/84 mmHg lying. He had a fine tremor. Investigations:

An ion channel linked to the PTH receptor
An ion channel linked to the PTH receptor is incorrect as PTH exerts its action via a G-protein-coupled receptor.

stem: A 25-year-old adopted man consults for review. He is interested in having children and is concerned about the possibility of inheritance of a genetic disease. You understand from adoption papers that his natural parents were Scandinavian, although they were not identified further. Which one of the following is most prevalent genetic disease in patients of Finnish/Scandinavian origin?
explanation:
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (A1AD)
Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (A1AD) or alpha-1 is a genetic disorder caused by defective production of alpha1 antitrypsin (A1AT), leading to decreased A1AT activity in the blood and lungs and deposition of excessive abnormal A1AT protein in liver cells. Around 4% of people of northern European descent carry the PisZ allele, and between 1 in 625 and 1 in 2000 are estimated to be homozygous. A number of codominant alleles have been identified, with M being the most common. Homozygous MM individuals have no increased risk of emphysema or liver disease.

Congenital hypothyroidism
Congenital hypothyroidism is incorrect. Congenital hypothyroidism has an incidence of between 1 in 3000 and 1 in 4000.

Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is incorrect. Cystic fibrosis has an incidence of approximately 1 in 2500 in the European population.

Phenylketonuria
Phenylketonuria is incorrect. Phenylketonuria is much rarer, within incidence of approximately 1 in 10 000 live births. Alpha-1 Antitrypsin DeficiencyYou are examining cases of homocystinuria in a family from the Republic of Ireland. Family members have presented with a range of symptoms including ligamentous laxity, learning difficulties and lens dislocation. Which of the following enzyme defects is the most likely cause of homocystinuria in this family?

Sickle cell disease
Sickle cell disease is incorrect. Sickle cell disease is of course very uncommon in the northern European population. Although it is seen in approximately 1 in 350 live births to parents of African origin, it is virtually unheard of where parents are white.

stem: You are examining cases of homocystinuria in a family from the Republic of Ireland. Family members have presented with a range of symptoms including ligamentous laxity, learning difficulties and lens dislocation. Which of the following enzyme defects is the most likely cause of homocystinuria in this family?
explanation:
Cystathionine ß-synthase (CBS) deficiency
CBS deficiency leads to reduced activity of the enzyme that is involved in the conversion of methionine to cysteine. Homocysteine and methionine then accumulate in tissues and interfere with the cross-linking of collagen fibres. The G307S mutation is the most common cause of homocystinuria in patients of Celtic origin; Guthrie testing has shown the incidence to be 1 in 344 000 worldwide, but it is much higher in Ireland (1 in 65 000). Inheritance is autosomal recessive. Half of patients are responsive to pyridoxine. Other cases of homocystinuria result from abnormalities in the conversion of homocysteine to methionine.

5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) deficiency
5,10-methylenetetrahydrofolate reductase (MTHFR) deficiency is incorrect. MTHFR deficiency is incorrect as although this can lead to high levels of homocysteine, it is much rarer in the Celtic population (being much more common in individuals of Mexican descent).

Glutathione peroxidise (GP) deficiency
Glutathione peroxidise (GP) deficiency is incorrect. GP deficiency is incorrect as this may contribute to a range of diseases, including vitiligo and haemolytic anaemia, and accelerate progression of diabetic nephropathy.

Glutathione synthetase (GS) deficiency
Glutathione synthetase (GS) deficiency is incorrect. GS deficiency is incorrect as this leads to haemolytic anaemia and oxoprolinuria; other symptoms which are manifest include neurological impairment and ataxia. HomocystinuriaMethionine synthase (MS) deficiency
Methionine synthase (MS) deficiency is incorrect. MS deficiency is incorrect as this presents with megaloblastic anaemia as the major consequence and may, in severe form, also be associated with neurological impairment.

stem: A 26-year-old man has autosomal recessive ecommon variable immunodeficiency. He would like to start a family, and his partner does not have the disease but has not been genetically tested. What is the percentage chance that this patient’s children will suffer from his disease?
explanation:
< 5%
All children of this patient will carry at least one gene for common variable immunodeficiency, but the chance of his partner carrying one copy of the gene is low; therefore, < 5% of his children will inherit the disease. The risk of being a carrier for common variable immunodeficiency is 1 in 30 000. Most patients with common variable immunodeficiency present as sporadic cases, although reports exist of familial cases with various inheritance modes, including autosomal dominant with variable penetrance, autosomal recessive and X-linked disease.

0%
Although the risk of this patient’s children suffering from the disease is very low, it is not zero. The prevalence of common variable immunodeficiency is 1 in 30 000. Therefore, there is a very small possibility that the man’s partner may have a single recessive gene, which would mean that the child may develop the underlying condition.

25%
25% is the risk of a child suffering from the disease in the event that both parents are carriers. This is because the child would have a 1 in 2, or 50%, chance of inheriting the recessive gene from both parents. This means 1/2´ 1/2, which leads to a 1/4, or 25%, chance of inheriting both recessive genes and having the condition.

50%
50% is the approximate risk of a child suffering from the disease if the mother was a carrier. This is because the father has two copies of the recessive gene, and the mother would have one normal copy and one copy of the recessive gene. Therefore, the child would definitely inherit one recessive gene from the father and has a 50/50 chance of inheriting a recessive gene from the mother. Genetic Counselling Including Patterns of Inheritance100%
100% is the risk of a child being a carrier of the disease if the partner is not a carrier. The only way the child would have a 100% chance of also having the condition is if both parents were heterozygous for the recessive gene (they both had two copies of the recessive gene). This does not take account of spontaneous mutations that may occur.

stem: Multiple members from a large family suffer from an autosomal dominant disorder. Although the gene for the condition is known, a mutation has not been found in the family. One of the family members wants to know if he will develop the disease as his father is affected. Blood samples are available from both affected and unaffected members. Which molecular technique is most useful in this situation?
explanation:
Linkage analysis
It is quite common for a gene mutation not to be found in a family even though the gene for the condition is known. Often this is due to the limitations of mutation screening (although sometimes a mutation in a different gene might cause the same phenotype). If a reasonable number of samples are available from affected and unaffected members of a family then linkage analysis can be performed using microsatellite markers. By testing both affected and unaffected members, the allele carrying the mutation can be tracked through the family.

Chromosome analysis
Chromosome analysis is incorrect. It is used to look at gross chromosome structure rather than for the purposes of gene analysis.

DNA sequence analysis
DNA sequence analysis is incorrect. DNA sequencing is a mutation detection technique.

Microarray analysis
Microarray analysis is incorrect. This is a gene expression technique. He smokes 15 cigarettes per day, works part-time as a stonemason, and takes a salbutamol and beclomethasone inhaler. What can the patient do to protect his lung function against further deterioration?

Southern blotting
Southern blotting is incorrect. Southern blotting is a mutation detection technique.

stem: A 31-year-old man with a history of alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency (A1AD; PiSZ type) is concerned about protecting his lung function for as long as he can. He smokes 15 cigarettes per day, works part-time as a stonemason, and takes a salbutamol and beclomethasone inhaler. What can the patient do to protect his lung function against further deterioration?
options: Intervention will not affect progression of lung disease
explanation:
Stopping smoking
In patients with PiSZ type A1AD, continued cigarette smoking massively increases progression of symptomatic lung disease. Across three studies of A1AD, the age at onset of dyspnoea was 48–54 years in non-smokers versus 32–40 years in smokers. In individuals with the PiSZ phenotype, cigarette smoking is a particularly important risk factor for the development of COPD, which rarely occurs in non-smokers with this phenotype.

Intervention will not affect progression of lung disease
Intervention will not affect progression of lung disease is incorrect. With PiSZ phenotype, obstructive lung disease is not a feature unless patients have a smoking history.

Maintain his inhaler therapy
Maintain his inhaler therapy is incorrect. Although a significant proportion of patients with A1AD also have asthma, maintaining his inhaler therapy is of much less importance with respect to outcomes versus smoking cessation.

Maintain regular exercise
Maintain regular exercise is incorrect. Pulmonary rehabilitation does impact on exercise tolerance and outcomes in patients with established disease, but in this case exercise will not slow progression of lung disease. Alpha-1 Antitrypsin DeficiencyStopping work as a stonemason
Stopping work as a stonemason is incorrect. Given adequate airways protection, working as a stonemason should not significantly impact on progression to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in patients with PiSZ type A1AD.

stem: A 17-year-old man comes to the endocrinology clinic with concerns that he isn’t entering puberty properly. His only past medical history of note is that he has no sense of smell. On examination, his BP is 105/70, a pulse of 68 and regular. He is slim and is 1.88m in height. He has gynaecomastia, sparse axillary and pubic hair, and small firm testes. Laboratory testing reveals a testosterone below the lower limit of normal. Which of the following additional features would favour a diagnosis of Kallman’s syndrome over Klinefelter’s syndrome?
explanation:
Anosmia
Anosmia raises the possibility of partial Kallmann’s syndrome, with failure of production of GnRH. Complete Kallmann’s syndrome, with failure to enter puberty, and partial Kallmann’s are both well described.

47 XXY karyotype
47 XXY karyotype is incorrect. This is consistent with a diagnosis of Klinefelter’s syndrome.

Gynaecomastia
Gynaecomastia is incorrect. Gynaecomastia is consistent with Klinefelter’s but is seen in 1/3rd or less of patients with the condition.

Low testosterone
Low testosterone is incorrect. Low testosterone can be observed in both Kallman’s and Kleinfelter’s syndromeand is a cause of premature osteoporosis in individuals with these conditions. Klinefelter SyndromeYou are on call and are contacted by the Gynaecology Registrar.

Sparse axillary and pubic hair
Sparse axillary and pubic hair is incorrect. Sparse pubic and axillary hair and small testes are well recognised features of Klinefelter’s syndrome.

stem: A 22-year-old woman with a diagnosis of Turner syndrome comes to the clinic for review. She enquires about her long-term future. From the following, of which are patients with Turner’s syndrome most at risk?
explanation:
Premature cardiovascular death
Turner’s is associated with significant cardiovascular pathology including aortic coarctation, bicuspid aortic valve, and aortic root dissection. There is also a 2–3-fold increase in hypertension in the Turner syndrome population. Given the risk of aortic root dissection, aggressive control of blood pressure is advised, accompanied by 5-yearly echocardiography. Reference: (

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect as although Turner syndrome patients are at risk of Type 2 diabetes, the incremental risk is slight. It is thought to be due to increased propensity for weight gain and insulin resistance in the Turner’s population.

Gynaecological cancer
Gynaecological cancer is incorrect as although gonadoblastoma is a risk in patients with Y chromosome material, only about 5% of patients with Turner’s are thought to have cells containing some Y chromosome material.

Renal failure
Renal failure is incorrect as although a range of anatomical abnormalities are found in the renal systems of patients with Turner syndrome – including horseshoe kidney, double-collecting ducts and complete absence of one kidney – given aggressive management of hypertension and absence of recurrent renal tract infections, the incidence of renal failure is not increased as much as the risk of cardiovascular death. Turner SyndromeThyroid cancer
Thyroid cancer is incorrect as hypothyroidism rather than thyroid cancer is the major risk in Turner syndrome.

stem: An obese 25-year-old man is referred to a dermatologist with fleshy nodules on the backs of his elbows. He also has yellow linear deposits in his palmar creases. His fasting serum lipids are: cholesterol 14.2 mmol/l, triglycerides 16 mmol/l. Fasting plasma glucose and thyroid function tests are normal. In addition to dietary and lifestyle advice, what would be the most appropriate treatment?
explanation:
A fibrate and a statin
The lipid deposits in the palmar creases, probable tuberous xanthomas on the elbows and elevations of cholesterol and triglyceride to approximately equal molar concentrations are typical of remnant hyperlipidaemia (familial dysbetalipoproteinaemia, broad beta disease). Fibrates with statins are usually an effective treatment for the condition. The dyslipidaemia is frequently expressed clinically because of an additional factor, for example impaired glucose tolerance or frank diabetes, and such conditions should be sought and treated appropriately if present.

A bile-acid sequestrant
A bile-acid sequestrant is incorrect. Bile-acid sequestrants reduce cholesterol but may increase triglyceride concentrations, they are also very unpalatable to take.

A statin
A statin is incorrect. Although high dose statins do reduce triglycerides at very high dose, they are primarily used for lowering LDL cholesterol.

Nicotinic acid
Nicotinic acid is incorrect. Nicotinic acid does lower cholesterol and triglycerides but is often poorly tolerated due to symptoms of facial flusing and itching. Tuberous SclerosisA 25-year-old patient of West African origin presents to the Emergency Department with shortness of breath, severe lethargy and jaundice. You understand he was recently prescribed an antibiotic by his GP for the treatment of gastroenteritis. On examination his BP is 100/70 mmHg; pulse is 85 bpm and regular. He looks pale and short of breath at rest. Abdomen is soft with mild tenderness. Investigations:

Omega-3 fish oils
Omega-3 fish oils is incorrect. Omega-3 fish oils are usually used to supplement fibrate therapy or as an alternative first line agent.

stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the clinic for review; he has significant arthritis with joint calcification, a bluish discoloration of his ear cartilage and passes urine that turns dark on standing. Other past medical history of note includes two episodes of lumbar disc herniation, the pain from which had settled over a number of weeks. Which of the following is the most likely underlying defect?
explanation:
Homogentisic oxidase deficiency
This patient has an autosomal recessive condition, homogentistic acid oxidase deficiency, which leads to alkaptonuria. It results from a set of inherited alleles on chromosome 3 (3q21-q23). It results primarily in symptoms of arthritis, and later cardiovascular disease: homogentistic acid is deposited in cartilage as a polymer and forms a black pigment layer. Attempts have been made to slow progression by restricting protein in the diet, although long-term data is not robust.

Alpha spectrin deficiency
Alpha-spectrin deficiency is incorrect. This results in hereditary spherocytosis, which results in chronic haemolysis, and patients may require splenectomy and cholecystectomy.

Glycogen synthase deficiency
Glycogen synthase deficiency is incorrect. This leads to symptoms of muscle cramps (particularly on exercise), ketosis and recurrent hypoglycaemia.

Glucuronyltransferase deficiency
Glucuronyltransferase deficiency is incorrect. This results in development of benign unconjugated hyperbilirubinaemia associated with Gilbert’s syndrome. Genetic Counselling Including Patterns of InheritanceA 17-year-old boy presented with absence of pubertal development. He had no other symptoms of note. On examination he was tall, his voice was unbroken, testes were small and there was only scanty pubic hair. His sense of smell is normal. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable.

Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency
Uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase deficiency is incorrect. This results in the development of porphyria.

stem: A 27-year-old woman comes to the genetics clinic. She is worried as her sister, mother and two aunts died of breast cancer. It is suspected that the family are carriers of the BRCA1 gene and she wants to know about the inheritance of BRCA1. Which one of the following fits best with BRCA1 inheritance in the majority of families?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
In the majority of families, BRCA1 is inherited in autosomal dominant fashion, as is BRCA2. BRCA1/2 carriers have a 40–70% chance of getting breast cancer by age 70, and a 10–70% chance of getting ovarian cancer by age 70. In comparison, the average woman has an 8% chance of getting breast cancer and a 1.5% chance of getting ovarian cancer by age 70.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. A number of autosomal recessive conditions, including ataxia telengiectasia, are associated with increased risk of breast cancer.

Mitochondrial disorders
Mitochondrial disorders is incorrect. Mitochondrial disorders are mainly associated with disorders of metabolism, exercise tolerance and progressive muscle weakness.

Sex-linked dominant
Sex-linked dominant is incorrect. Sex-linked dominant cancer syndromes are not widely described; an example of a sex-linked dominant condition is Alport’s syndrome. Genetic Counselling Including Patterns of InheritanceA 27-year-old man who has fragile X syndrome is having a child with another woman from the assisted living accommodation where he lives. She has cerebral palsy as a result of birth anoxia, but is not known to suffer from any inherited cause of learning disability. His partner attends for a 24-week scan and they find out they are expecting a daughter. What is the chance of the daughter inheriting the gene for fragile X?

Sex-linked recessive
Sex-linked recessive is incorrect. Sex-linked recessive disorders are not widely described as linked to cancer syndromes; bleeding disorders such as haemophilia A and B are X-linked recessive.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with severe hypertension and is found to have a unilateral phaeochromocytoma. His father died from metastatic renal cell carcinoma aged 48 and previously had surgery for a brain tumour. He has also had two pancreatic cysts identified on ultrasound scan. What is the most likely underlying genetic condition?
explanation:
von Hippel–Lindau disease (VHLD)
Complications of VHLD include phaeochromocytomas, renal cell carcinomas, and retinal and cerebellar haemangioblastomas, which can cause intracerebral haemorrhage. Both benign pancreatic cysts and neuroendocrine tumours are also seen in association with VHLD. Urinary catecholamine for phaeochromocytoma is recommended from age 10 in patients with VHLD.

Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT)
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is incorrect. This leads to arteriovenous malformations, including within the central nervous system (CNS), which can lead to significant bleeding, rather than increased risk of cancer.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A is incorrect. MEN 2A is associated with phaeochromocytoma, but not with increased risk of renal carcinoma.

Neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromatosis type 1 is incorrect. The absence of skin changes, including freckling, and neurofibromas counts against this diagnosis. Malignant transformation of neurofibromas is possible. Von Hippel–Lindau DiseaseYou are asked to see a 19-year-old man who has had recurrent pneumothoraces. He is tall with pes planus and has an increased arm span-to-height ratio and upper segment-to-lower segment body ratio. Which other feature would be most helpful in making a diagnosis of Marfan syndrome?

Neurofibromatosis type 2 (NF2)
Neurofibromatosis type 2 is incorrect. NF2 is primarily associated with increased risk of CNS tumours, including schwannomas and acoustic neuromas.

stem: A 17-year-old patient is 195 cm in height, slim, with a BMI of 21, and has a history of multiple previous joint dislocations and bilateral lens dislocation. Examination reveals arachnodactyly. He is diagnosed with Marfan’s syndrome. Which gene mutation is responsible for this condition?
explanation:
Fibrillin
Marfan syndrome is characterised by a triad of features: Long, thin extremities frequently associated with other skeletal changes, such as loose joints and arachnodactyly Reduced vision as the result of dislocations of the lenses (ectopia lentis) Aortic aneurysms that typically begin at the base of the aorta Most patients can be identified by detection of mutations in the fibrillin gene. Fibrillin-1 is a glycoprotein component of the extracellular matrix, and it is essential for the formation of that matrix, including the biogenesis and maintenance of elastic fibres. The extracellular matrix is critical for both the structural integrity of connective tissue and as a reservoir for growth factors.

Cyclooxygenase
Cyclooxygenase is incorrect. Cyclooxygenase deficiency is recognised and may result in bleeding disorders.

Galactosidase
Galactosidase is incorrect. Galactosidase deficiency results in the development of Fabry disease, leading to disordered metabolism of sphingolipids.

Hexosaminidase
Hexosaminidase is incorrect. Hexosaminidase deficiency results in neurodegenerative disease, such as Tay– Sachs, caused by a deficiency of β-hexosaminidase A. Marfan SyndromeA 17-year-old boy with a history of Type 1 diabetes mellitus, sensorineural high-tone deafness and colour blindness presents for review in the genetics clinic. You learn from his mother that other members of the family are affected, including a daughter aged 21 who also suffers from Type 1 diabetes. Which one of the following represents the usual mode of inheritance for the likely genetic syndrome?

Mitochondria
Mitochondria is incorrect as mitochondrial mutations commonly result in clinical disease characterised by progressive muscular weakness.

stem: A 17-year-old boy with a history of Type 1 diabetes mellitus, sensorineural high-tone deafness and colour blindness presents for review in the genetics clinic. You learn from his mother that other members of the family are affected, including a daughter aged 21 who also suffers from Type 1 diabetes. Which one of the following represents the usual mode of inheritance for the likely genetic syndrome?

stem: A woman who is 24 weeks pregnant with her first child has a brother with vitamin D-resistant rickets and wants to know the chances of her baby having the condition. She is well and has had an uneventful pregnancy so far. What is the approximate probability of the woman passing on the condition to her child?
explanation:
0%
Vitamin D-resistant (also known as hypophosphataemic rickets) carries X-linked dominant inheritance in the majority of cases. This patient, therefore, has zero chance of passing on the condition to her child, as by definition she must herself have two normal X chromosomes.

25%
25% is incorrect. 25% is the risk of inheriting an autosomal recessive disorder where both parents are carriers of the disease.

50%
50% is incorrect. 50% is the risk of children inheriting vitamin D-resistant rickets in the event that the patient herself was affected.

66%
66% is incorrect. 66% is the risk of being a carrier in the event that an individual has a sibling who is suffering from an autosomal recessive disease.

100%
100% is incorrect. This disease is an X-linked dominant disorder, meaning her risk of passing on the disease is only 50% if she had the condition herself, which she does not.

stem: A 40-year-old woman attends the clinic with her 9-year-old daughter. Her husband has recently died of a condition thought to be mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS), where he suffered a number of strokes with progressive dementia, and death at the age of 46. Which of the following represents the chances of her daughter being affected by the condition?
explanation:
0%
MELAS is a mitochondrial condition, and mitochondrial DNA is strictly conserved via the maternal line. As such, the chance of her inheriting MELAS is 0%, as she will not possess mitochondrial DNA from her father.

25%
25% is incorrect. 25% represents the chance of inheriting an autosomal recessive condition where both parents are carriers.

50%
50% is incorrect. 50% represents the chance of a child inheriting an autosomal dominant condition where one parent is affected.

66%
66% is incorrect. 66% represents the chance of being a carrier for a normal phenotype individual where a sibling is known to suffer from a recessive disorder.

100%
100% is incorrect. 100% represents the chance of carrier status for an X-linked recessive condition in daughters born to an affected father. Haemophilia A is an example of such an X-linked recessive condition.

stem: What is the importance of the P1 receptor?
options: Increasing cytotoxic drug excretion from cells
explanation:
Inducing apoptosis
P1 receptors are G-protein coupled membrane receptors preferentially bound by adenosine. There are a number of subtypes and thus a range of physiological effects. However, as a class the receptor is predominantly involved in mast cell function and eosinophil apoptosis – essentially functioning as a brake on an activated immune system

Calcium channel activator
Calcium channel activator is incorrect. Calcium channel receptors include L-type, T-type and ryanodine but not P1.

Increasing cytotoxic drug excretion from cells
Increasing cytotoxic drug excretion from cells is incorrect. Whilst some cells rely on secretion or efflux mechanisms to excrete cytotoxic drugs; these do not utilize the P1 receptor.

Increasing cytotoxic drug metabolite clearance
Increasing cytotoxic drug metabolite clearance is incorrect. Whilst a host of processes metabolite clearance, the P1 receptor is not implicated.

Potassium channel activator
Potassium channel activator is incorrect. Whilst a wide range of potassium channels exist including voltage gated, tandem pore domain, calcium activated and inwardly rectifying, the P1 receptor is not involved.

stem: You are examining patterns of inheritance across a range of genetic disorders. Which one of the following disorders is most likely to have an autosomal recessive mode of inheritance?
explanation:
Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
Kyphoscoliotic Ehlers–Danlos syndrome (kEDS), a specific subtype of EDS, is usually inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, meaning both gene copies must be mutated for a person to be affected. This condition involves severe muscle hypotonia at birth, progressive scoliosis, and hypermobility, among other symptoms caused by mutations in the PLOD1 or FKBP14 genes affecting collagen synthesis and stability. Parents who are carriers may show no symptoms but still pass on one copy of the defective gene, resulting in affected offspring if both parents contribute a faulty gene. Genetic testing and family history are essential for diagnosis and understanding inheritance patterns.

Achondroplasia
Achondroplasia is typically inherited in an autosomal dominant fashion, meaning that only one copy of the mutated gene from either parent can cause the disorder. This disorder results from mutations in the FGFR3 gene which affect bone growth leading to dwarfism. The majority of cases occur as new mutations with no prior family history due to a high mutation rate. Therefore, it does not follow an autosomal recessive pattern.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is inherited in an X-linked recessive manner, primarily affecting males because they have only one X chromosome, while females have two X chromosomes, providing a backup if one carries the mutation. The disorder leads to haemolytic anaemia triggered by certain medications, infections, or foods due to deficient enzyme activity protecting red blood cells from oxidative damage. Female carriers might show mild symptoms but generally do not experience severe effects seen in males unless they inherit two defective copies, which is rare given its X-linked nature; hence, it does not fit within autosomal recessive criteria.

Haemophilia A
Haemophilia A is inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern, which means the defective gene responsible for the disorder is located on the X chromosome. This type of inheritance primarily affects males, as they have only one X chromosome; a single altered copy of the gene will cause the disease. Females have two X chromosomes and typically are carriers if only one copy of the gene is mutated, often without showing severe symptoms themselves. Because this mode of inheritance involves sex chromosomes rather than autosomal chromosomes, it does not follow an autosomal recessive pattern.

stem: A 19-year-old man presents to the Emergency Department having suffered a sudden deterioration in vision. Additional past medical history of note includes bilateral shoulder dislocation. On examination he is tall and thin. On examination of his eye, the patient appears to have suffered a lens dislocation. Which of the following genes is most likely to be abnormal?
explanation:
Fibrillin-1
This man has Marfan syndrome: the history of joint and lens dislocation and his marfanoid habitus are strongly supportive of the diagnosis. Many cases are picked up in childhood however presentation can be delayed until early adulthood. Marfan syndrome occurs because of a defect in the fibrillin-1 gene, which codes for fibrillin, an essential building block of microfibrils, which are a component of the suspensory ligament of the lens and other tissues with elasticity, such as the aorta.

Collagen type II
Collagen type II is incorrect. Defects in the COL2A1 gene codes for collagen type II and is involved in the development of a range of cartilage development disorders.

Collagen type III
Collagen type III is incorrect. Mutations in the gene codes for collagen type III result in the development of vascular Ehlers–Danlos syndrome.

Collagen type IV
Collagen type IV is incorrect. Defects in the gene codes for collagen type IV are recognised to lead to the development of Alport syndrome. He informs you that his father had similar symptoms aged 50, his grandfather aged 75 and both deteriorated in terms of mobility and mental state, and eventually died. What is the phenomenon described here known as?

Collagen type V

stem: You see a 20-year-old woman with ataxia and restricted eye movements in the clinic. She tells you that she developed bilateral hearing loss at the age of 9 years, retinitis pigmentosa at 10 years and insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus at 15 years. When she was 18-years-old she had a pacemaker inserted for complete heart block. What is your diagnosis?
explanation:
Kearns–Sayre syndrome
This patient’s clinical features are typical of Kearns–Sayre syndrome, which is a mitochondrial disorder characterised by rearrangements of mitochondrial DNA, including deletions and duplications. The clinical features that suggest a mitochondrial disorder include any combination of sensorineural hearing loss, retinitis pigmentosa, muscle weakness, ataxia, recurrent stroke, cardiomyopathy, insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus, complete heart block and lactic acidosis. The tissues involved in mitochondrial disorders are those that depend heavily on oxidative phosphorylation for energy production. Kearns–Sayre syndrome is the only mitochondrial disorder of the five possible answers provided. Other mitochondrial disorders include myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibres (MERRF) and mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (together known as MELAS).

Friedreich’s ataxia
Friedreich’s ataxia is incorrect. This is an autosomal recessive disorder that initially manifests with symptoms of gait disturbance.

Myotonic dystrophy
Myotonic dystrophy is incorrect. This presents with facial and limb weakness, coupled with delayed muscle relaxation.

Spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA) type 7
Spinocerebellar ataxia type 7 is incorrect. SCA7 presents with progressive ataxia, motor system abnormalities, dysarthria, dysphagia and retinal degeneration.

Usher syndrome
Usher syndrome is incorrect. This presents with hearing loss and retinitis pigmentosa, without the other features seen here.

stem: A 26-year-old pregnant woman presents for her 24-week scan. It is her first child, and the father of her unborn child has haemophilia A. The scan shows that the child is a male fetus. The patient herself is well, and has no personal or family history or of bleeding disorders. Which one of the following represents the likely percentage chance that her son will have haemophilia A?
explanation:
0%
Haemophilia A is an X-linked disorder; hence, as the man supplies his Y chromosome to a male fetus, he does not increase the risk of the child being born with haemophilia above the background rate. As the prevalence of haemophilia A is around 20 per 100 000 male individuals, the risk of the baby being affected by haemophilia is close to 0.

25%
25% is incorrect. 25% is the risk of a child being affected by an autosomal recessive disorder where both parents are known to be carriers.

33%
33% is incorrect. 33% is the percentage chance of an individual not being a carrier of an autosomal recessive disease where siblings are affected by it.

50%
50% is incorrect. 50% is the risk of offspring of a sufferer of an autosomal dominant disease being affected by the condition. Haemophilia

100%
100% is incorrect. 100% is the risk of female offspring of this man being carriers of haemophilia.

stem: A man aged 33 presents with depression, weight loss and choreiform movements. He informs you that his father had similar symptoms aged 50, his grandfather aged 75 and both deteriorated in terms of mobility and mental state, and eventually died. What is the phenomenon described here known as?
explanation:
Anticipation
The phenomenon described here is known as genetic anticipation, where successive generations present with symptoms at an earlier age. It is known to occur in Huntington’s disease, the probable inherited illness seen here; although it occurs in affected men, affected women do not seem to show traits reflecting anticipation. Genetic anticipation is also seen in myotonic dystrophy and fragile X syndrome.

Autosomal dominance
Autosomal dominance is incorrect. Autosomal dominance merely refers to the fact that only one copy of an affected gene is required, driving a 50% chance of inheritance in children of an affected individual.

Increased penetrance
Increased penetrance is incorrect. Increased penetrance refers to the percentage of individuals who carry an abnormal gene who also express the phenotype.

Mitochondrial characteristics
Mitochondrial characteristics is incorrect. Mitochondrial characteristics can only be passed down via the female line. Huntington’s DiseaseA 26-year-old pregnant woman presents for her 24-week scan. It is her first child, and the father of her unborn child has haemophilia A. The scan shows that the child is a male fetus. The patient herself is well, and has no personal or family history or of bleeding disorders. Which one of the following represents the likely percentage chance that her son will have haemophilia A?

X-linked dominant characteristics
X-linked dominant characteristics is incorrect. These manifest with disease in both men and women, but the clinical phenotype is more severe in men. Alport’s is the prime example of an X-linked dominant disorder.

stem: A 22-year-old woman who is known to be a carrier of the haemophilia A genetic mutation comes to the clinic with her husband, who does not have haemophilia and has no past medical history of note. She has had a 20week scan for her first pregnancy and is having a boy. What is the risk that their child will suffer from haemophilia?
explanation:
50%
A male child inherits the X chromosome from the mother, where half of her X chromosomes carry the haemophilia A mutation; the chance of a male child having the disease is therefore 50%. As the condition is Xlinked recessive, no female children are affected by the condition, although 50% of them will be carriers for haemophilia. Mild/subclinical haemophilia may be seen in some female carriers due to X inactivation, so if female carriers are undergoing major surgery, it is advisable to measure baseline factor VIII activity.

0%
0% is incorrect as given the male child will inherit one X chromosome from the mother, the risk of suffering from the disease cannot be 0.

25%
25% is incorrect as this would be the inheritance risk if the condition was autosomal recessive and the father was also identified as a carrier.

75%
75% is incorrect as this is the risk of being a carrier or suffering from the disease in the offspring of two carriers of an autosomal recessive disorder. He has a past history of intussusception as a child, and two episodes of gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding over the past 15 years.

100%
