stem: You are asked to review a 17-year-old boy with massive weight gain and learning difficulties. On examination, you notice there is evidence of hypogonadism. As part of your assessment, you arrange for an assessment of peptide hormones to assess if any abnormality may be involved in the pathogenesis of his condition. Elevated levels of which one of the following is most involved in the pathogenesis of his condition?
explanation:
Ghrelin
The clinical picture here is of Prader–Willi syndrome which is associated with elevated ghrelin and hypogonadism. ghrelin is a hormone produced in the fundus of the stomach and in the pancreas ghrelin levels increase before meals and decrease afterwards receptors for ghrelin are found in the arcuate nucleus and the hypothalamus. Elevated ghrelin is thought to drive hyperphagia, which may well account for the clinical picture seen in Prader– Willi.

CCK
CCK is incorrect. Cholecystokinin (CCK) has been investigated as a weight loss agent and so would not cause the weight gain seen here. It is produced within the duodenum in response to nutrient load, and drives a reduction in appetite.

Leptin
Leptin is incorrect. Leptin is involved in satiety and so elevated levels would not result in weight gain. Leptin deficiency is thought to contribute to weight gain, and is involved in the pathogenesis of lipodystrophy. Replacement can therefore contribute to weight loss.

Secretin
Secretin is incorrect. Secretin has also been investigated as potential weight-loss agent so elevation is unlikely to result in this clinical picture.

Somatostatin
Somatostatin is incorrect. Elevated somatostatin is postulated to have a role in weight loss not gain.

stem: A 40-year-old man is referred to you with shortness of breath on minimal exercise over the past few months. He is now unable even to run for a bus. His GP has arranged an echo that shows an ejection fraction of 38%, and an ECG has revealed right bundle branch block and a prolonged PR interval. On examination you confirm his BP is 105/80 mmHg, and his pulse is 42 and regular. There are bilateral crackles on auscultation of the chest. You confirm bilateral ptosis, cataracts and a slowness to let go of your hand when you greeted him. He is estranged from his family and never knew his father, but he does know that his sister has a muscle problem and lost a child in infancy. What diagnosis might you suspect in this man?
explanation:
Myotonic dystrophy
Type 1 myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant neuromuscular disorder caused by an expansion in a triplet repeat in the DMPK gene. The degree of trinucleotide repeat expansion approximately correlates to the severity of the phenotype. Cardiomyopathy including conduction defects and bundle branch block are common. Other clinical features include myopathic facies, ptosis, myotonia, cataracts, testicular atrophy and diabetes mellitus. Genetic anticipation is seen across family groups with myotonic dystrophy type 1, although this is much less likely to be seen in type 2 myotonic dystrophy (related to a different expansion repeat in the CNBP gene). It is possible his niece had a very severe form of type 1 myotonic dystrophy, due to a massive expansion in the triplet repeat that is inherited from the affected mother.

Becker muscular dystrophy
Becker muscular dystrophy is incorrect. Becker muscular dystrophy can result in cardiomyopathy, although facial weakness is unusual. Proximal limb weakness is most often seen, with legs much more affected versus arms.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is incorrect. Duchenne’s presents with marked proximal limb weakness in childhood and is a life-limiting condition.

Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy
Facioscapulohumeral dystrophy is incorrect. This is most associated with bilateral weakness of the upper limb, which may be more marked on one side than the other, and weakness of the shoulders and face, rather than specifically the facial weakness seen here.

Spinal muscular atrophy
Spinal muscular atrophy is incorrect. Spinal muscular atrophy with adult onset presents with proximal limb weakness and decreased tone, rather than the increased tone seen here. You are asked to see a family with suspected Huntington's disease for genetic counselling. The family has come across the term 'genetic anticipation' on the internet.

stem: You review a 28-year-old man with a family history of early thyroid carcinoma and phaeochromocytoma. Your patient has been searching on the internet and has found information about the RET proto-oncogene and is worried about thyroid cancer. The RET proto-oncogene predisposes to which thyroid cancer?
explanation:
Medullary
Mutations of the RET proto-oncogene on chromosome 10 are associated with multiple endocrine neoplasia (MEN) 2A and 2B and familial medullary thyroid carcinoma. Multiple endocrine neoplasia MEN2A is associated with phaeochromocytoma, Cushing’s disease, medullary thyroid carcinoma and parathyroid hyperplasia. MEN2B is similar, but patients have a marfanoid habitus and intestinal and visceral ganglioneuromas, but not hyperparathyroidism; rarely, it may occur in isolation without other tumours. Medullary thyroid carcinoma Screening for medullary thyroid carcinoma is with pentagastrin and the calcium infusion test, with measurement of calcitonin. Where there is a family history of MEN2, total thyroidectomy in childhood to prevent the development of carcinoma is usually recommended. Prior to consideration of thyroidectomy, screening for coexistent phaeochromocytoma is essential, so that alpha blockade can be considered; otherwise the risk of on-table hypertensive crisis is high.

Anaplastic
Anaplastic is incorrect as this is a rapidly progressive thyroid carcinoma comprising poorly differentiated cells, and is primarily a disease of the elderly.

Follicular
Follicular is incorrect as this may be associated with familial cancer syndromes, including Gardner’s and Cowden’s.

Lymphoma
Lymphoma is incorrect as this is seen with increasing frequency in patients with Hashimoto’s thyroiditis.

Papillary
Papillary is incorrect as although familial papillary thyroid cancer does exist, it has been linked to mutations on chromosomes 1 and 8 rather than RET. Papillary thyroid cancer is also reported in association with Gardner’s and Cowden’s syndromes.

stem: A 30-year-old man is found to have three adenomatous polyps in the sigmoid colon at colonoscopy. He mentions that his father died at 45 with colon cancer, his paternal aunt was treated for rectal cancer at 45 and his paternal grandfather was treated for colon cancer at 50. He has no past medical history of note and general physical examination is entirely normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer (HNPCC)
This man’s family history fulfils the Amsterdam criteria for the diagnosis of hereditary non-polyposis colon cancer (HNPCC).According to these criteria, the diagnosis of HNPCC can be made in families with three or more affected individuals with colorectal cancer where: one affected individual is a first-degree relative (sibling, parent or child) of the other two; at least one affected individual is diagnosed before the age of 50 years; affected individuals are present in at least two generations; familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) has been excluded.The Amsterdam criteria have also been modified for use in smaller families and to take into account that women with HNPCC are at greater risk of endometrial cancer than colorectal cancer.

Cowden syndrome
Cowden syndrome is incorrect as although it is associated with increased risk of colorectal carcinoma, it is also associated with multiple hamartomatous polyps, which are clearly not seen here.

Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP)
Familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP) is incorrect as in FAP there are usually numerous polyps (more than 100 and often more than 1000) with a predominantly left-sided distribution.

Gardner syndrome
Gardner syndrome is incorrect as this is characterised by adenomatous polyposis of the colon, benign osteomas of the skull and facial bones, epidermoid cysts, dental abnormalities (odontomas, and supernumerary and impacted teeth), and desmoid and other tumours. Hereditary Non-Polyposis

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome
Peutz–Jegher syndrome is incorrect as this is associated with multiple hamartomatous polyps and perioral pigmentation.

stem: A 27-year-old woman presents with worsening back pain. As a child, she and her sister had several admissions to hospital with bone fractures following minor trauma, and she has recently developed bilateral hearing loss. Apart from some teeth discoloration and mild joint laxity, examination was normal. A vertebral X-ray showed partial collapse of L3. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Osteogenesis imperfecta is a dominantly inherited disorder of collagen, and this woman most probably has the type I (least severe) form. Type II is lethal in utero or shortly after birth, and type III is the severe form where affected individuals have hundreds of fractures and usually become wheelchair-bound. Clinical features include blue sclerae (not always present, as in this case), early-onset deafness and dentinogenesis imperfecta.

Early-onset osteoporosis
Early-onset osteoporosis is incorrect. This would not fit with dental changes or hearing loss. Additionally, there are no risk factors in the scenario to support a diagnosis of early osteoporosis.

Ehlers-Danlos syndrome
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome is incorrect. The classical type is typically associated with skin laxity and joint hypermobility but not with susceptibility to bone fractures.

Malignant bone metastases
Malignant bone metastases is incorrect. This would not fit with the hearing loss or dental changes seen here. You review a 19-year-old man who is referred to the clinic with recurrent nose bleeds. On examination you notice that he has multiple telangiectasias on his body and you are concerned that he may have an underlying genetic disorder. On further questioning you understand that one relative had a similar skin appearance and unfortunately died of a gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage, while another suffered from a stroke. What is the likely mode of inheritance for this condition?

Multiple myeloma
Multiple myeloma is incorrect. This is unlikely given she is 27 years old, and again does not fit with the hearing loss or dental changes.

stem: A 34-year-old man comes to the genetics clinic. He suffers from an inherited syndrome of diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus and deafness. His symptoms developed gradually over late childhood and into his teenage years. Given the suspected genetic basis of his syndrome, which other member of his family is likely to be affected?
explanation:
Mother
Inherited diabetes mellitus and deafness follows a mitochondrial inheritance pattern (the syndrome is known as DAD/MIDD). It differs from Wolfram syndrome in that there is no evidence of optic atrophy (Wolfram syndrome is considered as a prototype of endoplasmic reticulum diseases). All of the genetic material within mitochondria comes from the female line, and therefore his mother is the only member of those listed likely to have been affected. Other examples of mitochondrial diseases include Leber’s hereditary optic atrophy, MELAS (mitochondrial encephalopathy, lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes) and MERRF (myoclonic epilepsy with ragged-red fibres).

Daughter
Daughter is incorrect. Given the syndrome is mitochondrial, it is impossible for him to pass the syndrome onto his daughter, who will inherit all her mitochondrial DNA from her mother.

Paternal grandfather
Paternal grandfather is incorrect. It is impossible to pass any mitochondrial diseases via the paternal line.

Paternal uncle
Paternal uncle is incorrect. It is impossible to pass mitochondrial diseases via the paternal line, although daughters with fathers affected by X-linked recessive disorders do become carriers.

Son
Son is incorrect. The syndrome is mitochondrial, and so he will not pass any mitochondrial DNA onto his sons (similar to his daughters), as this comes solely from their mother.

stem: You review a 19-year-old man who is referred to the clinic with recurrent nose bleeds. On examination you notice that he has multiple telangiectasias on his body and you are concerned that he may have an underlying genetic disorder. On further questioning you understand that one relative had a similar skin appearance and unfortunately died of a gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage, while another suffered from a stroke. What is the likely mode of inheritance for this condition?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT), formerly known as Osler–Weber–Rendu syndrome, is inherited in autosomal dominant fashion. As such, a number of members in a patient’s family usually have a history of telangiectasias and recurrent bleeding episodes. It is thought to be related in many cases to a defect in a protein called endoglin, which is a receptor for transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β1) and has a role in tissue repair and angiogenesis. This is thought to lead to defects in endothelial junctions and perivascular tissue, which lead to telangiectasias. Mortality from HHT includes from GI haemorrhage, increased risk of haemorrhagic and ischaemic stroke, and high-output cardiac failure.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. Autosomal recessive telangiectasia is also recognised, but is associated with ataxia. It presents with progressive difficulty in co-ordination, usually at age less than 5.

Polysomic
Polysomic is incorrect. Polysomic inheritance occurs where there is an imbalance in chromosomal replication, often resulting in severe phenotypes and subfertility.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant is incorrect. X-linked disorders that lead to increased risk of bleeding include haemophilia A and B, which are inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect. X-linked disorders that lead to increased risk of bleeding include haemophilia A and B, which are inherited in an X-linked recessive pattern. Genetic.

stem: A 17-year-old man presents to the endocrinology clinic for review. He has significant weight gain, hyperflexibility and has difficulties with learning at school. You confirm marked obesity with a BP of 145/85 mmHG and pulse of 80 bpm. His BMI is 35. Routine bloods checked by the GP are unremarkable. You suspect a disease characterised by genomic imprinting. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Prader-Willi syndrome
The term 'genomic imprinting' refers to the dependence of the phenotype on whether the gene deletion is inherited from the mother or father. In PWS only the paternal copies of the genes which cause the syndrome on chromosome 15 are usually expressed, and their deletion, coupled with maintained ‘silence’ of the maternal genes, leads to the phenotype.

Huntington's chorea
Huntington’s chorea is incorrect. Huntington’s is characterised by trinucleotide repeats, with a 35–90 repeat segment of CAG nucleotides on chromosome 4p16.3. It presents in adulthood, often first with a mood disorder, followed by dementia and movement disorder, including marked choreiform movements. Huntington’s exhibits genetic anticipation, occurring earlier with successive generations.

Hurler syndrome type I
Hurler syndrome (type I) is incorrect. Hurler is an autosomal recessive disorder occurring due to a defect in chromosome 4p. It is characterised by intellectual disability, corneal clouding, deafness and cardiac disease, with death resulting in the first decade of life, often from cardiac disease.

Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome is incorrect. Marfan is autosomal dominant, due to a defect on chromosome 15, and is associated with ligamentous laxity/hyperflexibility, but not with the obesity and learning difficulties seen here.

Neurofibromatosis
Neurofibromatosis is incorrect. Neurofibromatosis is an autosomal dominant disorder with 95% penetrance; the gene is located on chromosome 17. Neurofibromatosis type 1 is associated with learning difficulties, but neurofibromas and café au lait spots which would be expected are not seen here.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner for genetic counselling after his brother was diagnosed with cystic fibrosis (CF). He is concerned about the likelihood of being a carrier and whether he should undergo genetic testing. Given the family history, what is the most likely pattern of inheritance for CF?
explanation:
Autosomal recessive
CF is inherited in an autosomal recessive manner, meaning that an individual must inherit two copies of the defective CFTR gene (one from each parent) to manifest the disease. Carriers have one normal allele and one mutated allele but do not exhibit symptoms. If both parents are carriers, there is a 25% chance with each pregnancy that their child will have CF, a 50% chance that their child will be a carrier like them, and a 25% chance that their child will neither be affected nor carry the mutation. Genetic counselling can help determine carrier status through specific genetic tests.

Autosomal dominant
This pattern involves only one copy of an abnormal gene needed to cause disease; thus, when a parent has an autosomal characteristic, half of their offspring will also have that trait. it typically appears in every generation if present within families. Examples include Huntington's disease and Marfan syndrome. However, this mode does not apply to CF as individuals who inherit only one copy of the CFTR mutation are merely carriers without symptoms.

Mitochondrial inheritance
Mitochondrial genes are inherited exclusively from mothers since mitochondria are passed on through oocytes but not spermatozoa. Diseases associated with mitochondrial DNA mutations affect cellular energy production but do not relate to CF as it involves nuclear DNA mutations, specifically in chromosome 7, affecting CFTR gene function.

X-linked dominant
Disorders caused by this mode appear due to mutations on the X chromosome where women (XX), having two X chromosomes, can be either heterozygous or homozygous for traits while men (XY), having only one X chromosome, exhibit more severe phenotypes if affected alleles are present because they lack a second compensatory allele on another X chromosome. An example includes Fragile X syndrome. However, this does not pertain to CF. Cystic Fibrosis A middle-aged woman is referred to you by her GP with a 6-month history of increasing breathlessness on exertion. Her son is affected with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, as was her brother. What would you be most concerned about in her?

X-linked recessive
This type affects mostly men who possess only one single copy of the mutated gene on their singular Xchromosome, leading them towards symptomatic manifestation, while women would require both copies altered, which occurs less frequently; hence, many become asymptomatic carriers instead, such as haemophilia A/B or Duchenne muscular dystrophy, unlike autosomal conditions including CF involving non-sex chromosomes entirely.

stem: A 34-year-old man attends the clinic with his partner. They are planning to start a family and are worried about risks of a child suffering from a genetic disorder. His partner is 29 years old. Which of the following disorders is the most common?
explanation:
Sex-linked disorder
The most common genetic disorder is actually a relatively minor one, red-green colour blindness, which is seen in 2–4% of men. Other examples of more significant sex-linked disorders include haemophilia A and B.

Autosomal dominant single-gene disorder
Autosomal dominant single-gene disorder is incorrect. An example of an autosomal dominant single-gene disorder is polycystic kidney disease, seen in around 1 in 1000 individuals.

Autosomal recessive single-gene disorder
Autosomal recessive single-gene disorder is incorrect. Autosomal recessive single-gene disorders are seen typically in 1 in 300 to 1 in 400 individuals; examples include haemochromatosis and cystic fibrosis.

Chromosomal disorder
Chromosomal disorder is incorrect. Chromosomal disorders are much rarer, given that many are not compatible with life.

A single polygenic disorder
A single polygenic disorder is incorrect. Polygenic disorders, including raised LDL cholesterol outside familial hypercholesterolaemia, are seen in approximately 1 in 100 individuals.

stem: A 55-year-old man presents to the Cardiology Clinic with progressive shortness of breath and occasional palpitations. On examination, there is a displaced apex beat and a third heart sound. His echocardiogram shows left ventricular wall thickness of 15 mm. What is the most likely underlying genetic cause?
options: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to MYH7 mutation
explanation:
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy due to MYH7 mutation
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM) is most commonly caused by mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins, such as MYH7, which encodes for beta-myosin heavy chain. This condition often presents with left ventricular hypertrophy on echocardiogram, as seen in this patient. HCM can lead to symptoms such as shortness of breath and palpitations due to abnormal myocardial architecture and diastolic dysfunction. Genetic testing can confirm the diagnosis by identifying specific mutations like those in the MYH7 gene.

Fabry disease
Fabry disease is an X-linked lysosomal storage disorder caused by deficiency of alpha-galactosidase A leading to accumulation of globotriaosylceramide in various tissues including the heart. Although it Chat can cause with AI cardiac Tutor manifestations like left ventricular hypertrophy, it typically also involves other systems with symptoms such as angiokeratomas, corneal opacities and acroparesthesia, which are not mentioned here.

Friedreich's ataxia
Friedreich's ataxia is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder caused by GAA repeat expansions in the FXN gene leading to frataxin deficiency. It frequently manifests with progressive ataxia and loss of proprioception before cardiac involvement appears; when present, cardiomyopathy tends to be dilated rather than hypertrophic.

Noonan syndrome
Noonan syndrome is a genetic disorder that affects multiple parts of the body, including distinctive facial features, short stature, and congenital heart defects such as pulmonary valve stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (obstructive or nonobstructive type) rather than isolated left ventricular hypertrophy seen here. Cardiomyopathy

Pompe disease
Pompe disease (Glycogen Storage Disease Type II) is another lysosomal storage disorder caused by acid alphaglucosidase deficiency, leading primarily to glycogen accumulation within muscle tissues, including cardiac muscle, causing hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. However, it typically presents earlier in life (infantile-onset form being more severe), often accompanied by generalised muscle weakness, which was not noted in this patient's presentation.

stem: An 18-year-old army recruit undergoes preliminary health screening and is found to have a Hb of 115 g/l (NR 130–170). Spherocytes are present in the peripheral blood film. Investigation of his siblings reveals that one of his two brothers also has spherocytic anaemia and had his gallbladder removed. In which one of the following is a defect most frequently responsible for this condition?
explanation:
Spectrin and Ankyrin
The diagnosis is hereditary spherocytosis, the most frequent cause of which is a mutation in the spectrin gene; spectrin is a component of the red cell membrane. The most common mutation in a Northern European population is a combined spectrin and ankyrin mutation, which is found in 40–65% of patients.

Actin
Actin is incorrect. Although actin mutations are associated with hereditary spherocytosis, they are less common in Northern European populations.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase is incorrect. Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency causes haemolysis when affected individuals are exposed to oxidising agents, which include a range of drugs.

Isolated Ankyrin
Isolated ankyrin is incorrect. Isolated β-spectrin mutations account for 15–30% of spherocytosis in Northern European populations, ankyrin mutations are less common.

Protein 4.2
Protein 4.2 is incorrect. Mutations in protein 4.2 may be found in populations such as the Japanese.

stem: A 24-year-old man with a history of sickle cell anaemia comes to the Emergency Department with a third vasoocclusive crisis in the past year. His treatment plan includes opioid analgesia, IV fluids and IV antibiotics. Which of the following would you most expect to find?
options: Presence of 70–90% HbS, 5–10% HbA and 2–20% HbF on electrophoresis
Clear appearance following sodium dithionite testing
explanation:
Hyposplenism
Sickle cell disease is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a substitution by the amino acid valine for glutamic acid on position 6. Recurrent vaso-occlusive crises result in splenic autoinfarction by adulthood for the majority of patients, leading to clinical evidence of hyposplenism.

Low reticulocyte count
Low reticulocyte count is incorrect. Microcytic hypochromic anaemia occurs in this condition with marked reticulocytosis (10–20%).

Thrombocytosis
Thrombocytosis is incorrect. Although thrombocytosis may be seen in sickle cell crisis, it is not as likely to be seen as hyposplenism.

Presence of 70–90% HbS, 5–10% HbA and 2–20% HbF on electrophoresis
Presence of 70–90% HbS, 5–10% HbA and 2–20% HbF on electrophoresis is incorrect. HbA is absent with 220% HbF and a predominance of HbS.

Clear appearance following sodium dithionite testing
Clear appearance following sodium dithionite testing is incorrect. HbS precipitates, leading to a turbid appearance on sodium dithionite testing. Sickle Cell Anaemia You are examining the potential for a resveratrol-derived compound to mitochondrial function.

stem: You are examining the potential for a resveratrol-derived compound to mitochondrial function. Which of the following would you expect to see as a response to the intervention in a clinical trial?
options: Decreased effects of the drug in the elderly
explanation:
Improved energy metabolism
Mutations in mitochondrial DNA lead to abnormalities in energy metabolism that can lead to impaired glucose tolerance, dyslipidaemia and muscle weakness. A number of compounds have targeted mitochondrial metabolism and these include resveratrol, a plant-derived phenol, and PPAR-delta agonists, although none have yet provided convincing evidence of efficacy.

Decreased effects of the drug in the elderly
Decreased effects of the drug in the elderly is incorrect as errors in mitochondrial DNA are thought to accumulate during life; any intervention, therefore, would be expected to have greater relative benefit in an elderly population.

Decreased HDL cholesterol
Decreased HDL cholesterol is incorrect as mitochondrial function improvements lead to an improvement in oxidative metabolism, which would be expected to drive a rise in HDL cholesterol.

Elevated triglycerides
Elevated triglycerides is incorrect as these are a feature of mitochondrial dysfunction.

Lipoatrophy
Lipoatrophy is incorrect as this is seen in response to drugs used in the treatment of HIV, which themselves drive mitochondrial dysfunction.

stem: You are mapping inheritance of a genetic disorder which appears to be passed from women to their offspring. You suspect this is due to a mitochondrial mutation. Which of the following diseases fits best with this pattern of inheritance?
explanation:
Leber’s optic neuropathy (LHON)
LHON was the first described disease associated with hereditary point mutations in mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA). It is characterised by subacute loss of binocular vision with a lesion of the central field of vision, improper colour vision and atrophy of optic nerve. Prevalence of mitochondrial diseases equals 1 : 10 000 of live-born infants. Mutations of mtDNA are their most frequent cause, often resulting in encephalomyelopathy, cardiomyopathy, vision disorders, dysacusis and metabolic disorders. Other examples of mitochondrial diseases include: Kearns–Sayre syndrome – caused by both deletions and duplications of mtDNA, the onset of disease symptoms is observed before 20 year of age. Short stature, pigmentary retinal degeneration, ophthalmoplegia, ptosis, ataxias, disturbances in conduction in heart muscle, diabetes and hearing loss all occur in the syndrome. Chronic progressive external ophthalmoplegia (CPEO) – may occasionally occur as a result of de novo mutation. Symptoms of CPEO include ptosis, myopathy, depression, cataract formation and ketoacidosis.

Alport syndrome
Alport’s syndrome is incorrect as this carries an X-linked inheritance pattern and occurs due to mutations in nuclear DNA.

Fabry disease
Fabry disease is incorrect as this is an X-linked disease caused by a mutation in nuclear DNA.

Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome is incorrect as this is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by a mutation in nuclear DNA.

Noonan syndrome
Noonan syndrome is incorrect as, like Marfan’s, this carries an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with fatigue, pruritus after a hot shower and splenomegaly on examination. Her full blood count reveals elevated haemoglobin and haematocrit levels. Which of the following genetic mutations is most likely associated with her condition?
explanation:
JAK2 V617F mutation
The JAK2 V617F mutation is most commonly associated with polycythaemia vera (PV), a type of myeloproliferative disorder characterised by increased red cell mass, leading to symptoms such as fatigue, pruritus after a hot shower and splenomegaly. This gain-of-function mutation in the Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) gene results in constitutive activation of the signalling pathway that promotes erythropoiesis independent of erythropoietin. Approximately 95% of patients with PV have this specific genetic alteration. Based on this patient's clinical presentation and laboratory findings, this is the most likely underlying genetic cause.

BCR-ABL1 translocation
The BCR-ABL1 fusion gene is characteristic of chronic myeloid leukaemia (CML) and is also known as the Philadelphia chromosome. It is not associated with polycythaemia vera or other classical myeloproliferative disorders like essential thrombocythaemia or primary myelofibrosis without the presence of significant leukocytosis or an elevated platelet count as seen in CML. This translocation leads to unregulated tyrosine kinase activity causing uncontrolled cell proliferation primarily affecting granulocytes rather than erythrocytes.

CALR mutation
Calreticulin (CALR) mutations are primarily found in patients with essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis rather than polycythaemia vera. These mutations are implicated when JAK2 mutations are absent but typically present differently from PV clinically as they do not predominantly cause increased red cell mass.

MPL W515L/K mutation
Mutations in MPL (myeloproliferative leukaemia virus) affect thrombopoietin receptor function and are more commonly associated with conditions like essential thrombocythaemia and primary myelofibrosis rather than polycythaemia vera. While it can be seen in some other forms of myeloproliferative disorders, it does not explain the constellation of symptoms, including elevated haemoglobin, which suggests polycythaemia vera is the more likely diagnosis.

SF3B1 mutation
Mutations in SF3B1 are frequently identified in cases involving refractory anaemias, such as those found within certain subtypes of Myelodysplastic Syndromes (MDS). They are not linked to classical Philadelphia chromosome-negative myeloproliferative neoplasms like polycythaemia vera, which presents differently both clinically and genetically.

stem: What is the most likely underlying genetic condition?
explanation:
Von Hippel Lindau syndrome
Von Hippel Lindau syndrome is caused by an autosomal dominant mutation in a tumour suppressor gene, leading to increased incidence of phaeochromocytoma. It increases the risk of renal cell carcinoma and pancreatic cysts: this patient’s father may have had both. Other features of von Hippel Lindau include bilateral epididymal cystadenomas in men, or of the broad ligament in women, and haemangiomas. Other genetic conditions linked to phaeochromocytomas are neurofibromatosis type 1 and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.

BRCA2
BRCA2 is incorrect. Carrying the BRCA2 mutation is associated with an increased risk of breast, ovarian and endometrial cancer, or prostate cancer in men, but it has no link to phaeochromocytomas. Genetic conditions linked to phaeochromocytomas include von Hippel Lindau syndrome (also associated with pancreatic cysts and renal cell carcinoma, as this patient’s father likely had), neurofibromatosis type 1, and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.

Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer
Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer is incorrect. This is also known as Lynch syndrome, and is an autosomal dominant condition conferring an increased risk of many types of cancers, including cancers of the bowel, endometrium, ovary, small intestine, hepatobiliary tract, urinary tract, central nervous system, and skin. However, it does not have an association with phaeochromocytomas. Genetic conditions linked to phaeochromocytomas include von Hippel Lindau syndrome (also associated with pancreatic cysts and renal cell carcinoma, as this patient’s father likely had), neurofibromatosis type 1, and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is incorrect. Type 1 is not associated with phaeochromocytomas; instead MEN type 1 is associated with pancreatic tumours (e.g. insulinomas, gastrinomas or VIPomas), parathyroid hyperplasia or adenomas, and pituitary tumours (mostly prolactinomas). MEN type 2 is associated with phaeochromocytomas (in addition to medullary thyroid carcinoma and parathyroid hyperplasia). The most likely underlying genetic cause in this patient is the autosomal dominant von Hippel Lindau syndrome. This syndrome is also associated with pancreatic cysts and renal cell carcinoma, as this patient’s father likely had.

Neurofibromatosis type 2
Neurofibromatosis type 2 is incorrect. NF2 is not associated with phaeochromocytomas: it is classically associated with bilateral acoustic neuromas, meningiomas and gliomas. Patients with NF2 usually have less marked cutaneous signs and are at increased risk of developing cataracts. However, neurofibromatosis type 1 is associated with phaeochromocytomas, along with cutaneous signs (neurofibromas, café-au-lait spots, axillary freckling), optic nerve gliomas, Lisch nodules, and renal artery stenosis. Other genetic conditions linked to phaeochromocytomas include von Hippel Lindau syndrome (also associated with pancreatic cysts and renal cell carcinoma, as this patient’s father likely had), and multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2. Von Hippel–Lindau.

stem: A 20-year-old man presents with pes cavus, distal weakness and wasting of his leg muscles, absent knee and ankle jerks and reduced sensation to touch, and vibration in his feet and legs. His father is said to have similar problems. Nerve conduction studies show absent sensory potentials from his sural nerve and significantly reduced motor-nerve conduction velocities in his common peroneal nerve. What is the most likely diagnosis?
options: Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 1 (HMSN 1)
explanation:
Hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy type 1 (HMSN 1)
The history, clinical findings and result of nerve conduction studies in this man are consistent with the diagnosis of HMSN 1. The family history is suggestive of an autosomal dominant disorder (male-to-male transmission). The clinical findings suggest that the patient has a mixed (motor and sensory) peripheral neuropathy, and this is confirmed by the results of nerve conduction studies that show absent sensory potentials from the sural nerve and reduced motor-nerve conduction velocity (NCV). The motor-nerve conduction velocity is reduced (ie < 38 m/s), and therefore this patient has HMSN 1.

Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia
Autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia is incorrect. There are no features described in the scenario here.

Dejerine–Sottas syndrome
Dejerine–Sottas syndrome is incorrect. This presents in childhood with delayed motor development, hypotonia, areflexia, ataxia, palpable peripheral nerves and motor NCVs < 10 m/s.

Friedreich’s ataxia
Friedreich’s ataxia is incorrect. This usually presents in late adolescence with ataxic gait as the initial feature. You see a healthy 20-year-old man in your clinic. There is no significant past medical history and he plays rugby for Saracens Rugby Club. He tells you that his brother died at the age of 7 years with cystic fibrosis (CF). What are his chances of being a carrier?

Hereditary neuropathy with liability to pressure palsies (HNPP)
HNPP is incorrect. This is associated with a predisposition to recurrent common peroneal nerve and/or ulnar nerve palsy as a result of pressure or traction. This condition can also be associated with a mild generalised peripheral neuropathy.

stem: A colleague asks for your help in designing a new diagnostic molecular assay where small amounts of DNA need to be accurately amplified. Which would be your technique of choice?
explanation:
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
PCR is a rapid and versatile method for amplifying defined target DNA sequences. It is one of the cornerstone techniques in molecular genetics and facilitates the rapid cloning and analysis of DNA. It uses a heat-stable polymerase enzyme originally derived from a species of thermophilic bacteria. A typical PCR reaction takes 1–2 hours. It is a fast, sensitive and robust technique, and has been adapted for a multitude of different applications.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)
Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay is incorrect. ELISA is not effective for defining DNA sequences, and is instead used to evaluate/examine for the presence of peptides and antibodies.

Immunoprecipitation
Immunoprecipitation is incorrect. It is used to precipitate a peptide out of solution by using an antibody which specifically binds to it.

Southern blotting
Southern blotting is incorrect. Being more complex and time-consuming, and largely superseded by PCR.

Western blotting
Western blotting is incorrect. Western blotting is used for protein, not DNA, characterization.

stem: A 64-year-old man presents for his annual diabetes review. He tells you he has missed his recent retinal screening appointment. You carry out fundoscopy. Which of the following options warrants urgent ophthalmology referral?
explanation:
Retinal detachment
Detachment of the retina may cause permanent blindness and should be regarded as a medical emergency.

Background diabetic retinopathy
Background diabetic retinopathy does not necessitate urgent treatment, but is usually monitored carefully for progression; optimization of diabetes treatment is essential.

Cataracts
Cataracts warrant non-urgent referral for surgical extraction.

Drusen
Drusen are normal in advancing age and do not require urgent treatment.

Non-proliferative changes in the periphery
Non-proliferative changes in the periphery, unless severe, do not require urgent referral. Mild and moderate non-proliferative diabetic retinopathy is generally not treated unless accompanied by clinically significant macular oedema.

stem: A couple aged in their early 30s come to the genetics clinic. They have one 6-year-old son who has gross obesity and mild mental impairment, diagnosed as Prader–Willi syndrome, and they are concerned about the possibility of further children being affected. Which one of the following most accurately describes the mode of inheritance of Prader–Willi?
explanation:
Non-Mendelian
Prader–Willi occurs because of deletion or disruption of genes on the proximal arm of the paternal copy of chromosome 15 (15q11–13). It is the first human disorder to be attributed to genetic imprinting, where genes are expressed differently based on which parent they came from. Around 70% of cases occur owing to deletion of 15q11–13, and 28% are due to maternal disomy. Prevalence of the condition is estimated as being as high as 1 : 8000 in rural Sweden, and as low as 1 : 25 000 in other areas. Features include morbid obesity, hyperphagia, hypogonadism and mental impairment.

Autosomal dominant
Autosomal dominant is incorrect. Autosomal dominant obesity is found in patients who have mutations in the melanocortin 4 receptor.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. A range of autosomal recessive syndromes exist that drive obesity, including PC1, NPY and ghrelin-receptor mutations.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant is incorrect. Wilson–Turner syndrome is an example of a rare X-linked dominant obesity syndrome, where patients present with intellectual disability, truncal obesity, gynaecomastia, hypogonadism, dysmorphic facial features and short stature.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect. Other similar syndromes to Wilson–Turner’s where the phenotype only occurs in men (ie X-linked recessive) have been described.

stem: A couple attended genetic screening for an inherited condition that has been observed in the husband’s family. He has muscle weakness affecting his face and the distal muscles of his arms and legs. There is delayed relaxation when you shake his hand. More severe cases have been observed in the family, with presentation at an earlier age. What is the most likely condition?
explanation:
Myotonic dystrophy
Myotonic dystrophy (MD) is an autosomal dominant disorder caused by the expansion of a cytosine–thymine– guanine (CTG) repeat that lies at the 3' end of the dystrophia myotonica protein kinase (DMPK) gene on 19q13.3. Normal individuals have fewer than 35 CTG repeats; affected individuals with MD generally have more than 50 CTG repeats. A CTG expansion of 50–80 repeats is associated with early-onset cataracts, and affected individuals with classical MD have larger CTG expansions. The most severe form of MD is congenital MD, which presents at birth with intrauterine growth retardation, severe hypotonia, muscle weakness and feeding difficulties. Children with congenital MD have developmental delay and learning difficulties, and develop myotonia in their teens.

Achondroplasia
Achondroplasia is incorrect. Achondroplasia occurs as a sporadic mutation in 80% of cases, otherwise it follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, and is associated with skeletal abnormalities rather than muscle weakness.

Becker muscular dystrophy
Becker muscular dystrophy is incorrect. Becker muscular dystrophy is associated with progressive proximal muscle weakness and calf muscle hypertrophy; it follows an X-linked inheritance pattern.

Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome is incorrect. Marfan’s is an autosomal dominant condition that is associated with ligamentous laxity rather than the muscle weakness seen here.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is incorrect. This presents with progressive muscle weakness and delayed motor milestones in early childhood.

stem: A 17-year-old patient has been investigated for recurrent bilateral shoulder and knee dislocation. He also complains of reduced vision and has suffered from previous lens dislocation. On examination he is very thin and is over 1.9 m tall. On general physical review he has a murmur consistent with mitral valve prolapse and arachnodactyly. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Marfan syndrome
Marfan’s is characterised by features that include significant ligamentous/joint laxity resulting in multiple joint dislocations, reduced vision related to lens dislocation and vascular abnormalities, including mitral valve prolapse, aortic regurgitation and eventually aortic aneurysm formation.

Osteogenesis imperfecta
Osteogenesis imperfecta is incorrect. Osteogenesis imperfecta is associated with musculoskeletal abnormalities due to multiple bone fractures, rather than recurrent joint dislocation.

Hypermobility type Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
Hypermobility type Ehlers–Danlos syndrome is incorrect. Hypermobility type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome is associated with recurrent joint dislocation, but not with tall stature and arachnodactyly.

Vascular type Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
Vascular type Ehlers–Danlos syndrome is incorrect. Vascular type Ehlers-Danlos syndrome, similar to hypermobility type Ehlers–Danlos, is not associated with tall stature and arachnodactyly.

Tay-Sachs disease
Tay-Sachs disease is incorrect. Tay-Sachs disease is a gangliosidosis, which presents with progressive neurological degeneration.

stem: A 17-year-old man comes to the haematology clinic for review. Following heavy bleeding after a tooth extraction, he is being investigated for a possible bleeding disorder that affects both male and female members of his family. Where is the most likely site of the defect?
explanation:
Chromosome 12
A bleeding disorder that affects both male and female members of the family fits best with a diagnosis of von Willebrand’s disease, which can follow both an autosomal dominant and an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern. The gene which codes for von Willebrand factor is found on chromosome 12.

Chromosome 1
Chromosome 1 is incorrect. An example of a gene located to chromosome 1 is the gene for variegate porphyria (the PPOX gene); it has an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance.

Chromosome 6
Chromosome 6 is incorrect. An example of a genetic disorder located to chromosome 6 is hereditary haemochromatosis. This is an autosomal recessive disorder with variable penetrance and results from a mutation of the HFE gene.

Chromosome 7
Chromosome 7 is incorrect. An example of a chromosome 7-related disorder is cystic fibrosis, caused by a mutation of the CFTR gene.

X chromosome
X chromosome is incorrect. Haemophilia, Duchenne and Becker forms of muscular dystrophy are all X-linked recessive conditions.

stem: A 22-year-old boy is diagnosed with the MODY-2 form of diabetes, like his father and sister before him. His physician explains that there is likely a genetic mutation affecting glucokinase. Glucokinase exists in brain, pancreas and liver, and responds differently in different locations. In the brain, the response is governed merely by different glucose levels, while in liver glucokinase activity increases after meals. Downregulation of glucokinase activity in the liver is an example of which one of the following?
explanation:
Co-repression
Glucokinase activity in the liver is downregulated by binding with glucokinase regulatory protein (GKRP). Co-repression is a term that relates to the fact that, by binding to GKRP, the action of glucokinase is downregulated or repressed. Small increases in glucose lead to the release of glucokinase from GKRP. In addition, insulin acts via SREBP1c to upregulate production of glucokinase, and a number of other promoter genes are also involved. Mutations in the glucokinase coding gene that lead to loss of function are responsible for MODY 2 (one of the forms of maturity-onset diabetes of the young).

Affinity
Affinity is incorrect. Affinity refers to the level of binding to glucose.

Co-activation
Co-activation is incorrect. Co-activation is the opposite of co-repression, where the presence of a co-factor leads to upregulation of activity.

Specificity
Specificity is incorrect. Specificity refers to how specific glucokinase may be for glucose or other sugars.

Stereoisomerism
Stereoisomerism is incorrect. Stereoisomerism implies that differing racemic forms of the enzyme may have different glucose activation thresholds.

stem: A 17-year-old girl comes to the endocrinology clinic with her parents. She has primary amenorrhoea. On examination her height is 145 cm and weight 45 kg. She is hypertensive with a blood pressure of 149/94 mmHg; pulse is 80 bpm and regular. She has a systolic murmur. Abdomen is soft and non-tender. BMI is 23. She has minimal breast development and sparse pubic and axillary hair. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Turner syndrome
The picture here with short stature, hypertension and a systolic murmur which might represent coarctation, coupled with primary amenorrhoea, raises the possibility of Turner syndrome. Other commonly seen features include short, webbed neck with a low hairline, a broad chest, cubitus valgus, short 4 th/5 th metacarpals and lymphoedema.

Crohn's disease
Crohn’s disease is incorrect. Although Crohn’s may be associated with poor weight gain and failure to enter puberty, the absence of abdominal pain and diarrhoea counts against this as the underlying diagnosis.

Cystic fibrosis (CF)
Cystic fibrosis is incorrect. There is no history of chest disease here, effectively ruling out CF as the cause of failure to enter puberty.

Iron deficiency anaemia
Iron deficiency anaemia is incorrect. We are given no suggestion of a mechanism for blood loss or an irondeficient diet in the scenario. Turner SyndromeMcCune-Albright syndrome
McCune–Albright syndrome is incorrect. In polyostotic fibrous dysplasia (McCune–Albright syndrome), precocious puberty causes premature closure of the epiphyses and short stature, but menstruation is not affected.

stem: How would you manage her von Willebrand’s pre-surgery?
explanation:
DDAVP® and tranexamic acid
DDAVP® will increase von Willebrand factor and factor VIII levels, while tranexamic acid is antifibrinolytic and will stabilise a clot that forms. N.B. A gene on chromosome 12 encodes the VW factor, a large multimeric molecule. VW factor is stored in Weibel–Palade bodies in endothelial cells and platelet α-granules. This protein is involved in platelet adhesion and is the carrier molecule for factor VIII, thereby preventing its premature destruction. Inheritance is autosomal dominant. Point mutations and major deletions of the gene have been described. Treatment Treatment includes: desmopressin (DDAVP®), which may boost factor VIII as well as VW factor levels factor VIII concentrates (Haemate P®), which contains significant amounts of VW factor antifibrinolytics, e.g. tranexamic acid

Blood transfusion
Blood transfusion is incorrect because it will not address the pathology in von Willebrand’s disease, which is a disorder of abnormal platelet adhesion associated with von Willebrand (VW) factor activity.

Transfusion of fresh frozen plasma
Transfusion of fresh frozen plasma is incorrect. Although fresh frozen plasma contains Von willebrand factor, it should be avoided as the patient has not been previously exposed to blood products.

Transfusion of Haemate P®
Transfusion of Haemate P® is incorrect because although Haemate P® contains a lot of factor VIII, this patient has not been exposed to blood products in the past. Therefore, if at all possible, she should not be exposed to blood products such as fresh frozen plasma or those from large donor pools, e.g. factor VIII concentrates.

Transfusion of platelets
Transfusion of platelets is incorrect because it will not address the pathology in von Willebrand’s disease, which is a disorder of abnormal platelet adhesion associated with von Willebrand (VW) factor activity.

stem: You are reviewing the pattern of neurological disease in a family of patients diagnosed with Huntington’s disease, a trinucleotide repeat disorder. Why has presentation become earlier in successive generations?
options: The phenotype is worse if the expansion is inherited by a man
The repeats expand from one generation to the next
There is ascertainment bias with younger family members diagnosed earlier
There is variable gene penetrance from generation to generation
explanation:
The repeats expand from one generation to the next
The repeats expand from one generation to the next, and it appears that paternal inheritance drives a larger number of repeats versus maternal inheritance. Patients tend to present with clinical Huntington’s when they have more than 35 repeats of the CAG sequence. In the 36–39 range they may or may not present with clinical disease; at 40 and above, presentation is invariable. Up to 120 or more repeats have been seen in patients presenting with very early disease. Other genetic diseases caused by abnormal triplet repeat expansion include myotonic dystrophy, fragile X, Friedreich’s ataxia, spinocerebellar ataxia and Kennedy’s disease.

Modifying genes exacerbate the phenotype
Modifying genes exacerbate the phenotype is incorrect. Gene–gene interaction may account for some variation in phenotype within families, but not for genetic anticipation.

The phenotype is worse if the expansion is inherited by a man
The phenotype is worse if the expansion is inherited by a man is incorrect. Inheritance of the repeat sequence from the father (paternal inheritance) does appear to drive even earlier presentation versus maternal inheritance.

There is ascertainment bias with younger family members diagnosed earlier
There is ascertainment bias with younger family members being diagnosed earlier is incorrect. This can contribute to earlier diagnosis (eg when mood disorders occur in early Huntington’s and they are no longer missed as a sign of underlying organic disease), but it does not completely account for earlier presentation. Huntington’s DiseaseThere is variable gene penetrance from generation to generation
There is variable penetrance from generation to generation is incorrect. This may account for intrafamilial variation, but not for successive earlier presentation with worsening severity.

stem: A 42-year-old woman presents to the General Practitioner with a family history of breast and ovarian cancer. She is concerned about her risk and wishes to undergo genetic testing. Which gene mutation is most likely associated with an increased risk for both breast and ovarian cancer?
explanation:
Breast cancer gene 1
Breast cancer gene 1 (BRCA1) is a tumour suppressor gene that, when mutated, significantly increases the risk of both breast and ovarian cancers. Women who carry mutations in the BRCA1 gene have up to a 72% lifetime risk of developing breast cancer and up to a 44% lifetime risk of developing ovarian cancer. The identification of BRCA1 mutations allows for targeted interventions, including more rigorous screening protocols, prophylactic surgeries, or chemoprevention strategies aimed at reducing these risks. Genetic counselling is also recommended for affected individuals to inform family members about their potential risks.

APC
The APC gene is a tumour suppressor gene. Its mutation is present in familial adenomatous polyposis and early onset of colon carcinoma. It is also found in aggressive benign tumours called desmoid tumours. However, it is not related to hereditary forms of breast or ovarian cancers.

BRAF
The BRAF gene encodes a protein called B-Raf which is involved in sending signals inside cells that are crucial for cell growth. Mutations in this gene are most commonly associated with melanoma but do not have strong associations with hereditary breast or ovarian cancers. Therefore, it would not be relevant in assessing hereditary risks specific to these cancers.

Epidermal growth factor receptor
Epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR), another oncogene implicated primarily in non-small cell lung carcinoma and certain other types of epithelial tumours like colorectal cancer, does not have strong links specifically connecting it with hereditary forms of breast or ovarian cancers. KRAS
KRAS mutations are typically involved in various forms of adenocarcinomas including pancreatic, colorectal, and lung cancers but again lack significant association with familial cases specifically involving both breast and ovary malignancies as seen prominently due to BRCA genes.

stem: When is a gene mutation causing a particular genetic disorder said to be completely penetrant?
options: When affected individuals with the same mutation have a very similar phenotype
When individuals with the mutation invariably develop the phenotype
When it affects a large number of the population
When it affects both sexes equally
When the disorder only manifests earlier in life in subsequent generations
explanation:
When individuals with the mutation invariably develop the phenotype
The penetrance is the proportion of individuals with the gene who show the phenotype; for example, Huntington’s disease shows a high penetrance as individuals with the mutation invariably develop the disorder The expression is the degree to which the disorder is manifested in the individual; for example, neurofibromatosis type I has a very variable expression, in that individuals can manifest in a variety of ways ranging from mild to severe

When affected individuals with the same mutation have a very similar phenotype
Option A is incorrect. Penetrance relates to whether an individual has the disorder phenotype, not the type of phenotype.

When it affects a large number of the population
Option C is incorrect. Penetrance relates to whether an individual has the disorder phenotype, not whether a large population is affected.

When it affects both sexes equally
Option D is incorrect. Penetrance relates to whether an individual has the disorder phenotype, not whether different sexes are affected differently. When the disorder only manifests earlier in life in subsequent generations
Option E is incorrect. Penetrance relates to whether an individual has the disorder phenotype, not at what age they get the disorder. This is anticipation.

stem: A 70-year-old Irish man is diagnosed with haemochromatosis. Subsequently, his son is also diagnosed with the condition. Both are homozygous for the common Northern European mutation. What is the most likely explanation?
explanation:
Pseudodominant inheritance
Psuedodominant inheritance is seen in populations where carriage of certain autosomal recessive conditions is particularly high. In this case the mother was a carrier of the same Northern European genetic mutation, giving a 50% chance of inheritance by any offspring with this male partner.

Autosomal dominant inheritance
Autosomal dominant inheritance is incorrect. Haemochromatosis type 4 carries an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern, although this is seen in African rather than Irish populations.

Mitochondrial inheritance
Mitochondrial inheritance is incorrect. Mitochondrial disorders are inherited through the female line. Examples include myoclonic epilepsy with ragged red fibres, and Leber’s optic atrophy.

Non-paternity
Non-paternity is incorrect. The presence of homozygosity in the son actually increases the likelihood that the older Irish man is the father. Hereditary Haemochromatosis

X-linked inheritance
X-linked inheritance is incorrect. Men cannot be homozygous for an X-linked condition because they carry one X and one Y chromosome.

stem: You are auditing the use of investigations in the hospital genetics clinic to establish the basis of a range of diseases. For which of the following genetic diseases is DNA analysis most likely to be diagnostic?
explanation:
Huntington’s disease
Huntington's disease is a trinucleotide repeat disorder, in which there is abnormal expansion of a cytosine– adenine–guanine (CAG) repeat that codes for a polyglutamine tract in the protein product called huntingtin. N-terminal fragments of mutant huntingtin accumulate and form inclusions in the cell nucleus in the brains of patients with Huntington’s disease, as well as in various animal and cell models of Huntington’s disease. DNA analysis thus allows quantification of the CAG repeats when this condition is suspected; the number typically increases in subsequently affected generations related to the proband, such that a second-generation carrier may present symptomatically at a younger age (the phenomenon known as ‘anticipation’).

Adult polycystic kidney disease
Adult polycystic kidney disease is incorrect. Adult polycystic kidney disease is most often associated with a mutation on the short arm of chromosome 16 and may be assessed genetically by DNA linkage analysis; but other mutations may also occur, limiting the utility of testing for a single-gene mutation.

Down syndrome
Down syndrome is incorrect. Chromosomal analysis is most appropriate in the assessment of Down syndrome.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is incorrect. Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy usually follows an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern. A wide range of genetic mutations have been identified, making testing for a single mutation less valuable.

Klinefelter syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome is incorrect as, like Down’s, Klinefelter syndrome is a chromosomal defect.

stem: You are asked to see a 19-year-old man who has had recurrent pneumothoraces. He is tall with pes planus and has an increased arm span-to-height ratio and upper segment-to-lower segment body ratio. Which other feature would be most helpful in making a diagnosis of Marfan syndrome?
explanation:
Early diastolic murmur
An early diastolic murmur indicates aortic valve incompetence, which is likely to be secondary to aortic root dilatation, a major feature of Marfan syndrome. Marfan syndrome is an autosomal dominant syndrome caused by mutations in the fibrillin-1 gene (FBN1) on chromosome 15q21, with an incidence of 1–2 per 10 000 Some 25% are new mutations and the gene is large and polymorphic, which makes diagnostic genetic testing problematic; the diagnosis is therefore currently made on clinical criteria Other major skeletal features include chest wall deformities (pectus carinatum or pectus excavatum) requiring surgery, a reduced upper segment-to-lower segment ratio, an arm span-to-height ratio > 1.05, a scoliosis of > 20 degrees and pes planus. Lens dislocation (usually upwards) is found in 50–80% of affected individuals. There is major skeletal criteria and minor skeletal criteria and for the skeletal system involvement in Marfan syndrome and for this to be used as criteria for the diagnosis, at least two major criteria or one major criterion plus two minor criteria must be present. Major skeletal criteria includes: 1) Pectus carinatum 2) Pectus excavatum (marked) 3) Reduced upper-to-lower segment ratio of less than 0.85 4) Increase arm span to height ratio (normal ratio is 1:1) 5) Positive thumb sign and wrist sign, also known as Steinberg sign and Walker–Murdoch sign 6) Thoracolumbar scoliosis (more than 20 degrees) 7) PCFD (progressive collapsing foot deformity) 8) Protrusio acetabula ( it is the migration of the femoral head along the femoral neck axis, medially and proximally, through the medial acetabular wall into the pelvis) Minor skeletal criteria include: 1) Moderate pectus excavatum 2) Hyper flexible joints 3) High vaulted palate (unusually high and narrow palate) 4) Specific facial appearance for example: hypoplasia, enophthalmos, retroganthia and malar hypoplasia etc.

Arachnodactyly
Arachnodactyly is incorrect. This is a minor criterion for diagnosis of Marfan syndrome.

High arched palate
High arched palate is incorrect. This is also a minor criterion for diagnosis of Marfan syndrome.

Joint hypermobility
Joint hypermobility is incorrect. Just as arachnodactyly and high arched palate, this is considered a minor criterion.

Mid-systolic click
Mid-systolic click is incorrect. This is suggestive of mitral valve prolapse, which is a minor criterion.

stem: A 28-year-old woman comes to the clinic. She is 24 weeks pregnant with a male fetus. Her partner is in good health, but her father suffers from haemophilia A. What is the percentage chance of the male fetus suffering from haemophilia A?
explanation:
50%
Haemophilia A is an X-linked recessive disorder. If the maternal grandfather of the child suffered from haemophilia A, then he would have passed the affected X chromosome on to his daughter. In turn, she has a 50% (1 in 2) chance of passing her affected X chromosome on to any male offspring she may have. Female offspring of carriers also have around a 50% chance of being carriers of the disease, depending on which X chromosome they inherit from the mother.

0%
0% is incorrect. 0% is the approximate risk of a male child being born with the condition if the mother is not a carrier and the father is the affected individual.

25%
25% is incorrect. 25% is the risk of a child being affected by an autosomal recessive disorder where both parents are known to be carriers.

33%
33% is incorrect. 33% is the percentage chance of an individual not being a carrier of an autosomal recessive disease where siblings are affected by it. Haemophilia

100%
100% is incorrect. 100% is the percentage chance of female offspring of a male sufferer being carriers of haemophilia.

stem: A 18-year-old man presents with tiredness, pallor and easy bruising. Direct questioning elicits a history of bony pain and a low impact fracture last year. Examination reveals painless splenomegaly. Basic investigations confirm aneamia and thrombocytopenia. Glucocerebrosidase activity in peripheral leukocytes is 9% of normal, confirming a diagnosis of Gaucher’s disease. Which serum enzyme elevation is most supportive of this diagnosis?
explanation:
Acid phosphatase
Gaucher’s disease is a rare, inherited and potentially fatal disorder characterised by decreased levels of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase. Acid phosphatase activity is high in serum, an important diagnostic confirmation. Glucocerebrosidase deficiency allows accumulation of the lipid glucocerebroside in lysosomes of the monocyte macrophage system, resulting in lipid engorged Gaucher’s cells with eccentric nuclei. These displace healthy, normal cells causing bone marrow infiltration, hepatosplenomegaly, organ dysfunction and skeletal deterioration.

Alkaline phosphatase (ALP)
Alkaline phosphatase (ALP) is incorrect. Whilst ALP is most commonly elevated in hepatic and bony disease it is non-specific.

Alkaline transferase (ALT)
Alkaline transferase (ALT) is incorrect. ALT elevation represents non-specific evidence of hepatocyte damage.

Aspartate transaminase (AST)
Aspartate transaminase (AST) is incorrect. transaminase AST) elevation represent non-specific evidence of hepatocyte damage. He is accompanied by his carer who says he has a chromosome abnormality. What type of abnormality is most likely to cause such a severe phenotype?

Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH)
Lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) is incorrect. Raised LDH levels can be found in malignancy, haemolysis, shock, myocardial infarction, liver disease, renal disease and a host of other processes.

stem: A 43-year-old woman is diagnosed with early cirrhosis and is found on further investigation to have haemochromatosis. She drinks no alcohol and her periods finished early at the age of 39. Her husband is not a carrier for the condition. What is the likelihood that her two young children will be carriers for the condition?
explanation:
100%
Haemochromatosis is an autosomal recessive disorder, which often presents later in women because they are generally protected from liver disease due to their menstrual cycle. A woman presenting with evidence of early cirrhosis at the age of 43 will almost certainly be homozygotic for the haemochromatosis mutation, or be a carrier of two different, co-existing haemochromatosis genes. This means that all of her children will be carriers for the haemochromatosis gene; the two most common mutations that have been identified are C282Y and H63D. Venesection is the initial treatment of choice.

0%
0% is incorrect. 0% is incorrect as given this is an autosomal recessive condition and she has presented very early very shortly after the menopause, she must carry two abnormal genes, making her chance of passing on the condition 100%.

25%
25% is incorrect. 25% is the chance of inheriting an autosomal recessive condition where both parents are carriers of the condition.

50%
50% is incorrect. 50% is the chance of inheriting an autosomal dominant condition in offspring of one affected parent.

66%
66% is incorrect. 66% is the chance of a sibling of a patient affected by an autosomal recessive condition being a carrier if they do not exhibit the associated phenotype.

stem: You are running the hospital genetics clinic and are consulted by parents who have a child with significant congenital defects. The parents want to have a further child and are concerned that the disease may be inherited through the female line of the family. Given this history you suspect there may be a mitochondrial inheritance pattern. Which one of the following features would be typical of a mitochondrial disorder?
explanation:
Optic atrophy
Features of mitochondrial disorders include optic atrophy, neuropathy, diabetes mellitus, epilepsy, diabetes insipidus and sensory neural hearing loss. They are inherited via the female line because it is mutations in mitochondrial DNA from the egg that are responsible.

Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis is incorrect. Bronchiectasis raises the possibility of Kartagener syndrome, which is related to a ciliary defect, or cystic fibrosis, which is related to a cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance receptor (CFTR) defect. Both follow an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern.

Hypercholesterolaemia
Hypercholesterolaemia is incorrect. Familial hypercholesterolaemia is inherited in autosomal dominant fashion.

Pseudohypoparathyroidism
Pseudohypoparathyroidism is incorrect. Inheritance of pseudohypoparathyroidism is in autosomal dominant fashion with parental imprinting.

Spina bifida
Spina bifida is incorrect. Familial cases of spina bifida are described, but in fact most cases are sporadic. The inheritance pattern in families has not been completely established.

stem: A 52-year-old woman presents to the hepatology clinic with symptoms of chronic liver disease. She maintains that she does not drink alcohol to excess and is found on genetic screening to have homozygosity for haemochromatosis. Neither of her parents was known to suffer from the disorder. Her sibling lives far away, and you know nothing of her past medical history. What is the probability that her sibling will be a carrier?
explanation:
50%
If the woman is homozygous, then each of her parents must have carried one gene for haemochromatosis. As such their offspring have a 25% chance of carrying no genes for the condition, a 25% chance of having the condition and a 50% chance of being a carrier.

0%
0% is incorrect. Although mutations leading to hereditary haemochromatosis are common, implying that a new mutation is possible, a homozygous new mutation would be very unusual, making 0% incorrect as the risk for her sibling.

25%
25% is incorrect. 25% reflects the probability that she would be both disease-free and not a carrier.

66%
66% is incorrect. 66.6% reflects the probability of the sibling being a carrier if we know that she does not suffer from the disease.

100%
100% is incorrect. Unless both of her parents suffered from haemochromatosis, 100% inheritance risk could not be achieved. Hereditary Haemochromatosis You are examining the inheritance pattern of a neurodegenerative disorder that appears to be genetic in origin.

stem: You are examining the inheritance pattern of a neurodegenerative disorder that appears to be genetic in origin. Which of the following is true of autosomal dominant (AD) and autosomal recessive (AR) inheritance?
options: Both parents are commonly unaffected in AD disorders
Three unaffected siblings and unaffected parents suggests AR inheritance
Trinucleotide repeats are usually seen in AR disorders
Variable penetrance is never seen in AD disorders
explanation:
Three unaffected siblings and unaffected parents suggests AR inheritance
Given a child of an affected parent has a 50:50 chance of being affected by an AD disorder, having three unaffected siblings implies AR inheritance. The fact that the parents are unaffected also excludes an AD disorder.

Both parents are commonly unaffected in AD disorders
Both parents are commonly unaffected in AD disorders is incorrect as this is impossible; at least one parent must have been affected by the disease.

Genetic anticipation suggests AR inheritance
Genetic anticipation suggests AR inheritance is incorrect as trinucleotide repeats are seen in Huntington’s, an AD disorder, and expansion of the repeats leads to genetic anticipation (presentation at an earlier age with subsequent generations).

Trinucleotide repeats are usually seen in AR disorders
Trinucleotide repeats are usually seen in AR disorders is incorrect as these are seen in autosomal dominant disorders such as Huntington’s. An obese 25-year-old man is referred to a dermatologist with fleshy nodules on the backs of his elbows. He also has yellow linear deposits in his palmar creases. His fasting serum lipids are: cholesterol 14.2 mmol/l, triglycerides 16 mmol/l. Fasting plasma glucose and thyroid function tests are normal. In addition to dietary and lifestyle advice, what would be the most appropriate treatment?

Variable penetrance is never seen in AD disorders
Variable penetrance is never seen in AD disorders is incorrect as more severe symptoms are seen in patients with AD trinucleotide repeat disorders, where there is an increase in the number of repeats with subsequent generations.

stem: A 35-year-old man is referred to you with altered bowel habit and weight loss. One of his sisters had a hysterectomy for uterine cancer aged 42, another sister had colorectal cancer aged 44 and his father died from colorectal cancer in his 50s. External physical examination is unremarkable. Colonoscopy shows a few polyps and a caecal mass. Which genetic condition might be running in the family?
explanation:
Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer
Hereditary non-polyposis colorectal cancer (HNPCC) is an autosomal dominantly inherited predisposition to colorectal cancer in the absence of florid polyposis. There are two main forms: Lynch I (no family history of other cancers) Lynch II (with other cancers in the family, eg endometrial, ovarian, urinary tract) It is diagnosed according to the ‘Amsterdam’ criteria: families must have at least three relatives over two generations with colorectal cancer, one a first-degree relative of the other two, with at least one case being diagnosed below the age of 50 years. These criteria were originally devised for research purposes and less stringent criteria are often used in clinical practice. At least six genes are known to cause HNPCC, and they are involved in repairing DNA sequence mismatches.

Familial adenomatous polyposis
Familial adenomatous polyposis is incorrect. This is characterised by profuse colonic adenomatous polyposis (much greater than that seen here); affected individuals develop hundreds of polyps by their second decade and have a greatly increased risk of colorectal cancer.

Neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromatosis is incorrect. This is associated with generation of multiple neurofibromas, and is not associated with increased risk of colorectal cancer.

Peutz–Jeghers syndrome
Peutz–Jeghers syndrome is incorrect. This is characterised by melanin flecks on the lips and mucocutaneous borders with a hamartomatous polyposis, and is associated with an increased risk of colorectal cancer. The normal facial appearance reported here counts against Peutz–Jegher’s as the underlying diagnosis. Hereditary Non-Polyposis

von Hippel–Lindau disease (VHLD)
von Hippel–Lindau disease (VHLD) von Hippel–Lindau disease is incorrect. VHLD is associated with increased risk of renal cell cancer and phaeochromocytomas.

stem: A 40-year-old man develops jerky, choreiform movements affecting his arms and legs. He has been treated with antidepressants over the past year for low mood. His father died at the age of 55 and had been diagnosed as having Huntington’s disease. Which one of the following genetic abnormalities is responsible for this condition?
explanation:
Triplet repeat mutation
Huntington’s disease, an autosomal dominant disease, is caused by a triplet repeat mutation, with expansion (typically 40–55 repeats) of the CAG triplet, leading to a significant increase in glutamine residues in a protein known as huntingtin. Huntington’s disease demonstrates ‘genetic anticipation’, particularly when inherited via the paternal line, with an increasingly early onset in succeeding generations: this is due to an increase in the number of triplet repeats. Huntington’s disease is inevitably fatal.

Frameshift mutation
Frameshift mutation is incorrect. Frameshift mutations occur because of insertions or deletions of nucleotides, and have been described in genetic diseases such as cystic fibrosis.

Point mutation
Point mutation is incorrect. Point mutation involves a change in a single nucleotide, an example of which is the C282Y mutation responsible for haemochromatosis.

Splicing mutation
Splicing mutation is incorrect. Splicing mutations are responsible for a range of other genetic diseases, including thalassaemia. A woman presents to the genetics clinic for review. She has von Willebrand's type 1 disease, and so does her partner. They both have mild difficulties with bleeding tendency, normally related to dental procedures. They are seeking information as to the risk of transmitting the disease to their offspring. How would the risk of disease transmission to her offspring be best described?

Termination mutation
Termination mutation is incorrect. Termination mutations result in generation of a premature stop codon. One example of a disease caused by a termination mutation is Hurler syndrome.

stem: A woman presents to the genetics clinic for review. She has von Willebrand's type 1 disease, and so does her partner. They both have mild difficulties with bleeding tendency, normally related to dental procedures. They are seeking information as to the risk of transmitting the disease to their offspring. How would the risk of disease transmission to her offspring be best described?
options: No offspring will have the disease
Half of the offspring will be carriers
Three-quarters of the children will have the disease
explanation:
Three-quarters of the children will have the disease
Von Willebrand’s type 1 is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner: if both parents have the disease, then three-quarters of their offspring will have the disease, assuming they are both heterozygotes.

All offspring will be carriers
All offspring will be carriers is incorrect. The disease is autosomal dominant, meaning there is in effect no carrier state.

No offspring will have the disease
No offspring will have the disease is incorrect. This is an autosomal dominant condition, meaning three-quarters of the offspring will be affected.

All sons will be affected
All sons will be affected is incorrect. The condition is not sex-linked, but autosomal dominant, and therefore it would be expected that three-quarters of sons will be affected.

Half of the offspring will be carriers
Half of the offspring will be carriers is incorrect. In an autosomal dominant condition, there is no carrier state.
