stem: A 28-year-old man who is starting a family has extensively researched the risk of him passing on a range of genetic diseases. Which of the following does he have the greatest risk of passing on to male offspring if he is found to have the abnormal gene associated with the condition concerned?
explanation:
Myotonic dystrophy
Myotonic dystrophy is an autosomal dominant condition resulting in a 50% risk to the male and female offspring of an affected man; therefore, this is the correct answer.

Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis is incorrect. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive condition resulting in a 25% risk of inheritance of the condition in the offspring of an affected man if the female partner is also a carrier of the condition.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy
Duchenne muscular dystrophy is incorrect. This is an X-linked condition where there is absence of male-to-male transmission, although all the daughters of an affected man will be carriers, and then they themselves are at risk of having affected sons.

Haemophilia type A
Haemophilia type A is incorrect. Haemophilia A is an example of an X-linked condition, meaning that male offspring of a man are not affected by the condition.

MELAS (myopathy, encephalopathy, lactic acidosis, stroke)
MELAS is incorrect. Neither male nor female offspring of an affected man will be affected as this is a mitochondrial disorder, meaning that abnormal mitochondria are only inherited via the woman’s ovum.

stem: An article in a leading medical journal reads: ‘an insertion of five nucleotides in the gene was identified as the cause of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy in this family’. Which one of the following types of mutation is the author referring to?
explanation:
Frame-shift mutation
As the group of nucleotides inserted is not a multiple of three, the mutation changes the frame in which translation occurs and hence the name ‘frame-shift mutation’. The other answers (repeat mutation, missense mutation, nonsense mutation and point mutation) are therefore incorrect. The genetics of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy affects 1 in 500 people; and shows an autosomal dominant pattern of inheritance. At least 11 genes have been identified, which encode sarcomere or sarcomere related proteins. Many different types of mutation have been detected, which this question tests your familiarity with. Mutation types: A missense mutation is an alteration in a nucleotide sequence that converts a codon for one amino acid into a codon for a second amino acid. An insertion mutation arises by the insertion of one or more nucleotides into a DNA sequence. A nonsense mutation is an alteration in nucleotide sequence that changes a triplet coding for an amino acid into a termination codon. A point mutation results from a single nucleotide change in a DNA molecule. Another type of mutation relevant for MRCP Part 1 is a read-through mutation, which changes a termination codon into a codon specifying an amino acid and hence results in read-through of the termination codon.

Repeat mutation
Repeat mutation is incorrect. A repeat mutation occurs when short DNA sequences are repeated a number of times. This may result in abnormal protein function.

Missense mutation
Missense mutation is incorrect. A missense mutation is an alteration in a nucleotide sequence that converts a codon for one amino acid into a codon for a second amino acid (codes for a different amino acid). This may result in a protein that functions abnormally or not function at all.

Nonsense mutation
Nonsense mutation is incorrect. A nonsense mutation is an alteration in nucleotide sequence that changes a triplet coding for an amino acid into a termination codon.

Point mutation
Point mutation incorrect. A point mutation results from a single nucleotide change in a DNA molecule.

stem: What is the most probable diagnosis?
explanation:
Acute intermittent porphyria
AIP is the most common type of acute porphyria and inherited in autosomal dominant fashion. It is more likely to be associated with symptoms in women, which may reflect prescription of oestrogens as an exacerbating factor. Treatment includes administration of glucose, but to avoid worsening hyponatremia, administration of D5NS (5% dextrose in normal saline) is recommended.

Diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA)
Diabetic ketoacidosis is incorrect. Although DKA can present with abdominal pain and vomiting, hypertension is unlikely (due to hypovolaemia), and the proximity to prescription of the OCP suggests this as an exacerbating cause.

Guillain–Barré syndrome
Guillain–Barré syndrome is incorrect. This commonly presents with ascending weakness occurring 1-2 weeks after a precipitating infection (respiratory or gastrointestinal [GI]), not reported here.

Polyarteritis nodosa
Polyarteritis nodosa is incorrect. Other features of vasculitis, including fever, malaise, weight loss and arthralgia, would be expected, as would some degree of renal involvement.

Sarcoidosis
Sarcoidosis is incorrect. Most sarcoidosis is either asymptomatic or presents with respiratory symptoms (cough or shortness of breath) +/- erythema nodosum. Presentation acutely with abdominal pain would be highly unusual.

stem: You are examining alleles that may result in different degrees of obesity. Which of the following best describes an allele?
options: Location of DNA on a chromosome
explanation:
One form of a gene
An allele is defined as one of a number of alternative forms of the same gene or same genetic locus. Genes may exist in a number of forms, which may lead to a gain of or a loss in function. With respect to diseases such as obesity and Type 2 diabetes, genetic polymorphisms are increasingly identified that lead to either gain in weight or deficient insulin release in response to a glucose challenge. Examples include the TCF7L2 mutation that leads to a loss of incretin effect and PPAR-gamma mutations that are associated with increased insulin resistance.

An alternative amino acid
An alternative amino acid is incorrect. Amino acid substitutions occur as a result of allelic variance.

An alternative nucleotide
An alternative nucleotide is incorrect. Alleles may exist because of one or a number of nucleic acid substitutions.

Location of DNA on a chromosome
Location of DNA on a chromosome is incorrect. The mapping of genes to a particular location on a chromosome merely describes their position rather than the difference between particular variants.

Mutated ribonucleic acid (RNA)
Mutated ribonucleic acid (RNA) is incorrect. Allele is a term used to describe variations in a gene rather than changes in RNA.

stem: A young couple are referred to the Genetics Clinic for review. They have a child who has been diagnosed with achondroplasia and want information about the risks of any children that they may have in the future also having the disease. Both parents are of normal height. Which of the following represents the risk of the couple's future children having the disease?
explanation:
<1%
<1% 80% of cases of achondroplasia occur due to a new mutation, and because of germline mutation, the risk of further children suffering from the condition is less than 1%. It is an autosomal dominant condition.

0%
0% is incorrect. The risk is not 0%, but it is low given that 80% of cases come from new mutations.

25%
25% is incorrect. 25% is the risk of inheritance of an autosomal recessive condition where both parents are carriers.

50%
50% is incorrect. This is the chance the children of two carriers of a recessive disease being carriers themselves. Genetic Counselling Including Patterns of Inheritance100%
100% is incorrect. This is the chance of children from a sufferer of an autosomal recessive disease either being carriers or suffering from the disease themselves.

stem: A 28-year-old woman visits the genetic clinic because she is keen to start a family. Her brother has a diagnosis of cystic fibrosis (CF) and both her parents are confirmed unaffected carriers of the delta-F508 allele. She wants to know about her chances of being a carrier for the CF gene. She currently has no respiratory symptoms and neither of their parents exhibit symptoms. What is her chance of being a carrier of the delta-F508 allele?
explanation:
66%
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder; hence, both the maternal and paternal copies of the genes are required to develop the disease. There are three possibilities with respect to her genotype, given that she is now an adult and does not suffer from the disease: She will have inherited two normal genes from her parents (33%) She will have inherited one normal gene and the maternal CF gene (33%) She will have inherited one normal gene and the paternal CF gene (33%) Therefore, her chances of being a CF carrier is 33% plus 33% which is 66%.

25%
25% is incorrect. 25% is the risk of a child developing CF if both of the parents are confirmed as carriers.

33%
33% is incorrect. 33% is the chance of this patient having two normal genes and therefore not being a carrier for CF.

50%
50% is incorrect. A child who has parents who are both carriers have a 50% chance of being a carrier, 25% chance of not being a carrier and 25% chance of being affected by the condition. However this patient is now an adult and ha no symtoms of CF and is therefore likely to either be a carrier or not have a copy of the gene.

100%
100% is incorrect. Patients suffering from cystic fibrosis suffer from subfertility. If they do succeed in conceiving a child, these individuals have a 100% chance of their children becoming carriers, assuming their partner is clear of clinical CF disease and is not a carrier.

stem: A 20-year-old woman presents with hypothyroidism. On further questioning it transpires she has primary amenorrhoea. She is also of relatively short stature compared with her sisters. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Turner syndrome
Although Turner (XO), Down and Noonan syndromes can be associated with short stature and hypothyroidism, Down and Noonan syndromes are not associated with menstrual irregularities; hence, Turner syndrome is the most likely diagnosis here. The other typical features of Turner syndrome are cardiac defects (eg coarctation of the aorta), congenital lymphoedema, neck webbing, widely spaced nipples and cubitus valgus

Achondroplasia
Individuals with achondroplasia are usually very short; the condition does not have an increased incidence of hypothyroidism or menstrual irregularities

Down syndrome
Although Down syndrome can be associated with short stature and hypothyroidism, it is not associated with menstrual irregularities.

Noonan syndrome
Noonan syndrome is incorrect. Although Noonan syndrome can be associated with short stature and hypothyroidism, it is not associated with menstrual irregularities. Noonan syndrome is an autosomal dominant condition (so it affects both sexes), and other typical features include pulmonary stenosis, neck webbing and low-set posteriorly rotated ears Turner SyndromeA young couple are referred to the Genetics Clinic for review. They have a child who has been diagnosed with achondroplasia and want information about the risks of any children that they may have in the future also having the disease. Both parents are of normal height. Which of the following represents the risk of the couple's future children having the disease?

XXX syndrome
XXX syndrome is incorrect. Women with an extra X chromosome (XXX syndrome) are usually tall, nor does the condition have an increased incidence of hypothyroidism or menstrual irregularities.

stem: A 27-year-old man who has fragile X syndrome is having a child with another woman from the assisted living accommodation where he lives. She has cerebral palsy as a result of birth anoxia, but is not known to suffer from any inherited cause of learning disability. His partner attends for a 24-week scan and they find out they are expecting a daughter. What is the chance of the daughter inheriting the gene for fragile X?
explanation:
100%
The inheritance pattern for fragile X most closely resembles X-linked dominance with variable penetrance. Women who carry the defective X chromosome may have no signs of mental impairment at all, or demonstrate a mild degree of cognitive impairment and the other features of fragile X such as ataxia. For males (XY), if one parent has the affected gene, the chance of disease expression will also be 100%. In general X-linked recessive genes are more common than X linked dominant genes. While X-linked recessive genes have a predominance among sons (due to only one copy of the X chromosome), affected children in X-linked dominant genes is mostly determined by which parent carries the gene.

0%
0% is incorrect. This is the chance of a male child of a male patient with fragile X suffering from the condition.

25%
25% is incorrect. This is the risk of a child being affected by an autosomal recessive disorder where both parents are known to be carriers.

33%
33% is incorrect. This is the percentage chance of an individual not being a carrier of an autosomal recessive disease where siblings are affected by it. Fragile X Syndrome

50%
50% is incorrect. This is the percentage chance of a female carrier of the fragile X gene passing it on to a male or female child.

stem: A 25-year-old woman presents to her General Practitioner for a consultation. She is pregnant and concerned as she never received screening for rare diseases when she was an infant. Her partner has no significant medical history. She is currently well but recently learnt that her sister died of cystic fibrosis. Her chest X-ray is normal. Assuming a population carrier frequency of 1 in 25, what is the probability of her child contracting cystic fibrosis?
explanation:
1 in 150
Cystic fibrosis (CF) is an autosomal recessive disorder. In this scenario, the patient wants to enquire about the chances of having a child with CF. In this case, the father of the child does not have CF; therefore, he can either be a carrier or both of his genes are normal. Based on the population carrier frequency, he has a 1 in 25 chance of being a carrier. Therefore, his chance of passing the gene will be 1/25 multiplied by 1/2, which will be 1/50. The mother of the child had a sibling with CF. This means that both of her parents must be a carrier of the CF gene. If X = CF gene and x = normal gene, the maternal grandfather of the child = Xx. The maternal grandmother of the child = Xx. The vignette also states that the mother of the child is healthy. This means that her genetic makeup can be Xx, xX or xx. She cannot be XX because she is healthy. So there are three possible outcomes in total – 2 out 3 times, she will be a carrier; and 1 out of 3 times, she will have normal healthy genes. The chance of passing a carrier gene will be 2/3 multiplied by 1/2, which will be 1/3. Hence, the chance of having a child with the disease will be 1/3 multiplied by 1/50 = 1/150.

1 in 10
1 in 10 is greater than the carrier frequency for the general population and therefore cannot be correct.

1 in 50
1 in 50 is the chance of the male partner passing on an affected gene (1 in 25 x 1 in 2), assuming that they are free of cystic fibrosis.

1 in 100
1 in 100 implies a 1 in 2 chance of the mother passing on an affected gene, which must be incorrect, bearing in mind that we know she is not suffering from CF. Cystic Fibrosis

1 in 200
A probability of 1 in 200 implies a 1 in 4 chance of the mother passing on an affected gene.

stem: An 18-year-old student is referred to the Haematology Clinic for review. He has been referred to the clinic by the Emergency Department having suffered a large haemoarthrosis following a football injury, following which he was found to have reduced factor VIII activity, but at the > 5% level. He is due to undergo extraction of wisdom teeth. Which one of the following is the most important initial intervention with respect to his management?
options: He should be given desmopressin periprocedure
He should be given fresh frozen plasma (FFP) periprocedure
No intervention is needed for the tooth extraction
He should be given factor VIII periprocedure
He should be given cryoprecipitate periprocedure
explanation:
He should be given desmopressin periprocedure
This patient has mild haemophilia A (> 5% of activity), which means he is only at significant risk of bleeding associated with trauma or surgery such as tooth extraction. Desmopressin should boost factor VIII activity enough to avoid the need for exogenous administration.

He should be given fresh frozen plasma (FFP) periprocedure
He should be given FFP periprocedure is incorrect. Although FFP does replace clotting factors, desmopressin followed by recombinant factor VIII, if required, would be the first-choice interventions.

No intervention is needed for the tooth extraction
No intervention is needed for the tooth extraction is incorrect. Without desmopressin the risk of bleeding is significant.

He should be given factor VIII periprocedure
He should be given factor VIII periprocedure is incorrect. This is only required if there is bleeding despite use of desmopressin.

He should be given cryoprecipitate periprocedure
He should be given cryoprecipitate periprocedure is incorrect. Cryoprecipitate does contain factor VIII, but it would only be used realistically if recombinant factor VIII was unavailable and desmopressin had failed to stabilise bleeding.

stem: A 17-year-old man comes to the clinic for review. He was recently admitted to the Emergency Department with a shoulder dislocation. A past history of poor vision due to lens dislocation, behavioural difficulties and learning difficulties is noted. Apparently his father and mother both suffer from ischaemic cardiovascular disease. On examination his BP is 122/72 mmHg, pulse is 75/min and regular. He has crowded teeth, a high arched palate and marfanoid body habitus. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following is the most important intervention to prevent progression of disease in this patient?
explanation:
Pyridoxine supplementation
The clinical picture as described is consistent with homocystinuria. It is likely that this man’s parents were heterozygotes, suffering from hyperhomocysteinaemia, associated with premature ischaemic cardiovascular disease. Management of homocystinuria involves pyridoxine, folic acid and B 12 supplementation in combination, in an attempt to reduce homocysteine levels by methionine dietary restriction.

Ascorbic acid supplementation
Ascorbic acid supplementation is incorrect. It is not indicated. Ascorbic acid is recognised asChat a treatment for with methaemoglobinaemia, and is also a cause of elevated oxalate excretion and consequent renal stones.

B12 supplementation
B 12 supplementation is incorrect. Although some homocystinuria may also be responsive to B 12 supplementation, this may be added to pyridoxine, but the primary intervention is pyridoxine supplementation.

Folate restriction
Folate supplementation, not restriction, may be used in combination with pyridoxine for the treatment of homocystinuria. HomocystinuriaYou are examining alleles that may result in different degrees of obesity.

Cystine restriction
Cysteine restriction is incorrect. Cystinosis is a condition characterised by increased cysteine excretion and urinary stone formation. Cysteamine is the treatment of choice for cystinosis, driving cysteine breakdown and reducing overall cysteine levels by forming cysteine and cysteamine mixed disulphide, which can then be exported by lysosomes.

stem: A middle-aged woman is referred to you by her GP with a 6-month history of increasing breathlessness on exertion. Her son is affected with Duchenne muscular dystrophy, as was her brother. What would you be most concerned about in her?
explanation:
Cardiomyopathy
Female carriers of Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) may develop symptomatic cardiomyopathy, with a 10– 20% lifetime risk of developing the disorder. Cohort studies suggest that 80% of women and girls above the age of 16 years have at least early changes consistent with myocardial involvement, although the majority do not have symptoms of cardiac dysfunction. In boys, DMD (an X-linked condition) is diagnosed between the ages of 3 and 6 years with difficulty walking and calf pseudohypertrophy. Death occurs due to cardiomyopathy and/or respiratory failure by age 30. CK is always grossly elevated in conjunction with clinical disease.

Bronchiectasis
Bronchiectasis is incorrect. Type II respiratory failure to muscle weakness is seen in patients with clinical DMD. Bronchiectasis is of course seen with increased frequency in patients who are carriers of the cystic fibrosis gene.

Emphysema
Emphysema is incorrect. Emphysema is associated with alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency, not with DMD.

Pericardial effusion
Pericardial effusion is incorrect. Cardiomyopathy rather than pericardial effusion is a feature of DMD carriage.

Respiratory muscle failure
Respiratory muscle failure is incorrect. Respiratory muscle failure is seen in male patients with clinical DMD.

stem: A 17-year-old girl presents to the Emergency Department with downward dislocation of her right lens. She has learning difficulties and has suffered a left leg deep venous thrombosis but has no other past medical history of note. On examination, she is tall (185 cm), looks pale and her BMI is 21. She has crowded teeth and a higharched palate on examination of her mouth. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Homocystinuria
The clinical picture described above is in keeping with a diagnosis of homocystinuria. Homocystinuria is associated with increased risk of venous thrombosis, learning difficulties, lens dislocation and a Marfanoid habitus. Lens dislocation occurs downwards in homocystinuria, although it occurs upwards in Marfan’s.

Marfan's syndrome
Marfan syndrome is incorrect. Patients with Marfan do not have increased risk of venous thrombosis or learning difficulties, but are much more likely to be affected by cardiac defects than patients with homocystinuria.

Ehlers–Danlos syndrome
Ehlers–Danlos syndrome is incorrect. This is a disorder of connective tissue, and in particular of collagen. The commonest associated features include hypermobile joints, poor scar formation and stretchy skin. Spinal problems, osteoarthritis and cardiovascular disorders are common complications.

Maple syrup urine disease
Maple syrup urine disease is incorrect. This autosomal recessive disorder of metabolism of amino acids typically causes a distinctive sweet odour of the affected infant’s urine and presents with rapidly progressive neurological dysfunction.

Cystinosis
Cystinosis is incorrect. Cystinosis is a completely different disease to homocystinuria and is characterised by the abnormal accumulation of the amino acid cystine. The disease may manifest with renal, ocular and neurological symptoms, as well as diabetes and thyroid problems.

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents to the Cardiology Clinic with recurrent episodes of palpitations and syncope. Her ECG shows a prolonged QT interval, but genetic testing for congenital long QT syndrome (LQTS) returns normal results. What is the most likely chance that her offspring will inherit her condition?
explanation:
Unknown
Given that the patient has a prolonged QT interval but normal genetic testing, it suggests that her condition may not be due to one of the known genetic mutations associated with LQTS. This could indicate an idiopathic or acquired form of long QT syndrome, where environmental factors or other non-genetic elements might play a role. Since no specific mutation has been identified in this patient, we cannot accurately predict whether her offspring will inherit the condition. The risk remains unknown as it depends on whether a yet-to-be-identified genetic factor or purely environmental elements are responsible.

0%
This option assumes the complete absence of any inheritable component, which is incorrect since there may still be unidentified genetic factors at play. Even though current tests show normal results, they do not account for all possible mutations or inherited predispositions related to LQTS.

25%
This percentage would correspond to an autosomal recessive inheritance pattern if both parents were carriers of a recessive gene. However, without identifying any specific mutation in this patient’s genetics and given that only she presents with symptoms, assigning such a probability is inappropriate.

50%
A risk of 50% would suggest an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern where one parent carries one copy of the mutated gene sufficient to cause LQTS in each child independently of their partner's genotype or the percentage of carriers' offspring in case of autosomal recessive inherited diseases. As there are no identifiable mutations found in this patient’s case so far, assuming such a hereditary risk is premature without further evidence.

75%
There is no known mechanism by which LQTS could exhibit such high transmission rates under standard Mendelian inheritance patterns observed so far (dominant/recessive). Furthermore, overestimating risks without precise identification leads to misguidance especially given negative test results.

stem: A 19-year-old woman is referred to you with a blood pressure of 180/130 mmHg. On examination she has café au lait patches and some axillary freckling. There are multiple small fibrous lesions affecting her arms, legs and torso. She required surgery for scoliosis as a child. Her BMI is 23. What is the most likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1) is an autosomal dominant condition diagnosed in an individual who has met two or more of the following criteria: Six or more café au lait macules over 5 mm in greatest diameter in prepubertal individuals, and over 15 mm in greatest diameter in post-pubertal individuals Two or more neurofibromas of any type, or one plexiform neurofibroma Freckling in the axillary or inguinal regions Optic glioma Two or more Lisch nodules (iris hamartomas) A distinctive osseous lesion, such as sphenoid dysplasia or thinning of the long-bone cortex with or without pseudoarthrosis A first-degree relative (parent, sibling or offspring) with NF1 as defined by the above criteria. NF1 is due to mutations in the NF1 gene on chromosome 17q11, and is one of the most commonly dominantly inherited conditions. Hypertension can be caused by renal artery stenosis or phaeochromocytomas. Other complications include optic gliomas, vertebral dysplasia, pseudoarthrosis, intracranial tumours and malignant peripheral nerve-sheath tumours. About half of the people with NF1 have a learning disability.

Cushing’s disease
Cushing’s disease is incorrect as it is associated with significant weight gain, hypertension and diabetes, rather than the picture seen here with a BMI in the normal range.

Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is incorrect as it is not associated with the skin features seen here, nor with this level of hypertension.

Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome is incorrect as it is associated with excessive height, arachnodactyly and ligamentous laxity.

Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is incorrect as it is associated with hypopigmented macules, periungual fibromas, facial angiofibromas and shagreen patches (raised connective tissue lesions usually on the lower back). Other features include cortical tubers in the brain, learning disability, epilepsy and renal angiomyolipomas.

stem: A patient with known Alport syndrome who is the father of a 12-year-old girl attends the genetics clinic with his new partner. His daughter suffers from mild sensorineural hearing loss and dipstick-positive haematuria. The father wants to start a new family with his second partner and wishes advice regarding the chances of further children being affected by the disease. He tells you that out of other affected relatives, men seem much more severely affected than women, with a number of them having required renal replacement therapy before the age of 40 years. Given the history above, what is the most likely mode of inheritance of his daughter's condition?
explanation:
X-linked dominant
The 12-year-old girl has X-linked dominant Alport syndrome, in which women may present with dipstickpositive haematuria and hearing impairment, but are much less likely than men to suffer from gross haematuria and an increased risk of progression to kidney disease. Men with X-linked Alport syndrome, as observed in the family described here, are affected more severely, with approximately 90% of them progressing to kidney disease by age 40 years.

Autosomal dominant
Autosomal dominant is incorrect. The pattern of differential disease severity between men and women counts against an autosomal dominant disorder.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. Although Alport syndrome can follow an autosomal recessive pattern, men and women are equally, severely affected when family histories are examined.

Polysomic
Polysomic is incorrect. Polysomic inheritance occurs where there is an imbalance in chromosomal replication, often resulting in severe phenotypes and subfertility.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect. X-linked recessive disease does not produce a phenotype in women.

stem: A 23-year-old man of East African origin is admitted with anaemia. He has a condition where the amino acid valine, instead of the normal glutamic acid, has been substituted at position 6 of the β-globin chain. Which one of the following types of congenital haemolytic anaemia is he most likely to be suffering from?
explanation:
Sickle cell anaemia
Sickle cell anaemia is due to the inheritance of a gene for a structurally abnormal β-globin chain subunit of adult haemoglobin, HbS as opposed to normal HbA.The abnormal globin chain occurs because of a valine substitution for glutamic acid at position 6 of the β-globin chain.

β-thalassaemia
β-thalassaemia is incorrect. β-thalassaemia as this is due to a failure to synthesise the β-globin chain.

Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase (G6PD) deficiency is incorrect. This leads to haemolytic anaemia due to G6PD deficiency where mild (60–100%) to severe (< 10%) G6PD activity is seen.

Hereditary spherocytosis
Hereditary spherocytosis is incorrect. This is caused by a red cell membrane defect. In a Northern European population, the most common defect is a combined spectrin and ankyrin deficiency.

stem: A man in his mid-50s is referred to you because he is worried about his family history of ischaemic heart disease. He has recently retired and wants to maintain physical activity into retirement. His father was a nonsmoker and died of a myocardial infarction (MI) aged 39 years. His maternal grandfather and a paternal uncle both had myocardial infarcts in their 40s. What is his history most suggestive of?
explanation:
Familial hypercholesterolaemia
Familial hypercholesterolaemia affects around 1 in 500 of the population and is associated with a significantly increased risk of cardiovascular disease. Patients who are heterozygous for the condition present with early myocardial infarction in their 40s.

Factor V Leiden mutation
Factor V Leiden mutation is incorrect. Factor V Leiden mutation is most associated with increased risk of venous thromboembolism.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. Haemochromatosis is associated with increased risk of iron overload, which precipitates diabetes, endocrine deficiencies, hepatic cirrhosis and cardiomyopathy.

Homocystinuria
Homocystinuria is incorrect. Homocystinuria is an autosomal recessive inborn error of methionine metabolism and is associated with a greatly increased incidence of atheroma. Affected individuals often have a marfanoid habitus, and downward lens dislocation is also a wellrecognised feature. However, the autosomal recessive inheritance pattern would not fit with this family history.

stem: A 36-year-old man who was adopted at birth comes to the neurology clinic for review. Over the past year he has suffered from increasing forgetfulness and been treated by his GP for low mood and anxiety. He apparently traced his parents and found that his father died by suicide at the age of 52. Choreiform movements and clumsiness have also been noted. Routine bloods and a CT head are unremarkable. Which one of the following is the optimal way to screen for the likely underlying diagnosis?
explanation:
Polymerase chain reaction (PCR)
There is a suspicion here of underlying Huntington’s disease, given the suicide of his father, adoption of the child and presentation of this patient with neurological symptoms at a younger age, hinting at genetic anticipation. In this situation PCR represents the easiest way to screen for the disease, with triplet primed assays having been developed.

Northern blotting
Northern blotting is incorrect. Northern blotting is designed to detect ribonucleic acid (RNA) in a sample, and is therefore not relevant to the diagnosis of Huntington’s here.

Western blotting
Western blotting is incorrect. Western blotting is designed to evaluate protein expression, and may have a role in evaluating presence or absence of specific peptides associated with genetic diseases.

Restriction fragment length polymorphism (RFLP) testing
RFLP testing is incorrect. RFLP testing was the forerunner to PCR, is more complex and time-consuming, it has therefore been largely replaced.

Eastern blotting
Eastern blotting is incorrect. Eastern blotting is designed to evaluate post-translational modification of proteins, such as by lipidation of phosphorylation. Huntington’s.

stem: A 28-year-old man with Wilson's disease attends the genetics clinic with his wife as they wish to start a family. The carrier frequency in the average British population is 1 in 100, and his wife does not have the condition. They want to know the chances that they will have a child affected by Wilson's. Which of the following is the chance that their child will be affected by the condition?
explanation:
1 in 200
Wilson’s disease is an autosomal recessive disorder; as such, two abnormal genes are required for the male partner to develop the condition. We know that the female partner does not have Wilson’s, so she has a 1 in 100 chance of carrying one abnormal gene, and a 50% chance of passing on that abnormal gene; the chance of their child suffering from Wilson’s is therefore 1 in 200.

1 in 100
1 in 100 is incorrect. This is the chance of the female partner being a carrier of Wilson’s, rather than the chance of her offspring having the disease.

1 in 500
1 in 500 is incorrect. 1 in 500 is incorrect as this would approximate to 1 in 400, or the chance of having a child with Wilson’s if the husband was a confirmed carrier rather than suffering from the disease itself.

1 in 1000
1 in 1000 is incorrect. This is too low to represent the chance of inheriting Wilson’s even if the husband was a carrier rather than suffering from the disease.

1 in 2000
1 in 2000 is incorrect. This would fit with a carrier frequency for Wilson’s of 1 in 1000, rather than the 1 in 100 found in the British population. Genetic.

stem: A 35-year-old man presents with a 1-year history of choreiform movements, personality changes and mild memory loss. His father died with similar problems at the age of 50, and his uncle killed himself shortly after his father died. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Huntington’s disease
Huntington’s disease as it (also known as Huntington’s chorea) is the most likely diagnosis in this patient. This is an autosomal dominant disorder that usually presents in the third or fourth decade of life with personality change, dementia and chorea. It is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder leading to death about 15 years after onset. The cause is expansion of a cytosine–adenine–guanine (CAG) triplet repeat in the Huntington’s disease (HD) gene on 4p16. Normal repeat numbers are 9–35, and affected individuals have ≥ 36 repeats; a greater number of repeats is thought to drive earlier presentation with more severe disease.

Alzheimer’s disease
Alzheimer’s disease is incorrect. Patients with Alzheimer’s disease usually present after the age of 50 years with slowly progressive dementia; mood changes and minor deficiencies of short-term memory are initial presenting features. Chorea is not a feature of this condition

Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease
Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease (CJD) is incorrect. Patients with sporadic CJD present with progressive dementia and usually die within 2 years of onset of the disease. Although cases of new variant CJD present at a younger age, the prevalence of this condition has diminished significantly. Sporadic CJD is a disease of theChat elderly. with Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration
Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration is incorrect. Pantothenate kinase-associated neurodegeneration is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disorder that usually presents in childhood or adolescence and is characterised by: pyramidal and extrapyramidal signs dementia optic atrophy ‘eye of the tiger’ sign on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) scan of the brain due to the deposition of iron in the basal ganglia.

Wilson’s disease
Wilson’s disease is incorrect. This is an autosomal recessive disorder where most adult patients present before their mid-20s with a movement disorder, personality changes and Kayser–Fleischer rings on clinical or slit-lamp examination. They may also be detected via routine liver function test (LFT) monitoring. Huntington’s.

stem: A 21-year-old man presents to the Genetics Clinic for review. He is concerned about his risks of inheriting Huntington’s disease. His father recently died by suicide at the age of 43 after developing progressive neurological dysfunction with depression, choreiform movements and progressive rigidity. Genetic analysis reveals that he has 26 cytosine, adenine and guanine (CAG) repeats (normal range 10–35). Which of the following approximates to his percentage chance of developing Huntington’s?
explanation:
0%
We know that this patient’s number of CAG repeats is normal, and his chance of developing symptoms of Huntington’s is therefore 0%. Where patients consent to undergo a genetic test, a minimum of three sessions of counselling is recommended. Depression is common in patients with Huntington’s, and the risk of suicide is highest (5–10% of individuals with the disease) when symptoms first begin.

100%
The number of CAG repeats is closely related to the risk of developing Huntington’s disease. These are found within a gene called the huntingtin (HTT) gene on chromosome 4. Huntington’s is inherited in autosomal dominant fashion, and patients with over 40 CAG repeats will develop symptoms of the disease at some stage. The disease also exhibits anticipation, where an increasing number of repeats may be associated with presentation at an earlier age. There are no recognised therapies at present. In this case, in an autosomaldominant disorder, the chance of the man having inherited his father’s condition is 50%.

66%
66% does not fit with inheritance of a dominant disorder and is therefore incorrect. The risk of developing Huntington’s is proportional to the number of CAG repeats. In patients with 36 and 39 CAG repeats, there is less certainty that they will develop symptoms of Huntington’s. Symptoms may develop late in life or not at all.

50%
Although 50% is the chance of inheriting an autosomal-dominant disorder, we are already given the number of CAG repeats, which we know are below the upper limit of normal. This means that the patient will not inherit symptoms of Huntington’s disease.

25%
25% is incorrect, this is the percentage chance of developing an autosomal-recessive disorder when both parents are carriers of an affected gene. In Huntington’s, an autosomal-dominant disorder, the chance of inheriting the condition is 50%. Huntington’s.

stem: A 27-year-old Jewish man attends the clinic with his wife. They are keen to start a family but are worried because his brother developed jaundice during teenage years and was given a diagnosis of Dubin–Johnson syndrome. He asks for advice as to the chances of his children inheriting the condition. Which one of the following most accurately represents the mode of inheritance for Dubin–Johnson syndrome?
explanation:
Autosomal recessive
Dubin–Johnson’s is a rare cause of conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia, with a prevalence of around 1 : 1300 in Iranian Jews, the population with the highest prevalence. The cause is a genetic mutation of the human canalicular multispecific organic anion transporter (cMOAT) protein, also known as the multidrug resistance protein. It results in impaired transport of non-bile salt organic anions, which results in conjugated hyperbilirubinaemia. Over the long term the condition follows a benign course.

Autosomal dominant
Autosomal dominant is incorrect. Autosomal dominant hyperbilirubinaemia does occur in Gilbert syndrome where inheritance is via a missense mutation in the UGT1A1 gene. Gilbert’s does also carry autosomal recessive inheritance where the mutation is in the promoter region of the UGT1A1 gene.

Occurs by new mutation only
Occurs by new mutation only is incorrect. The new mutation rate is not well characterised, but given the condition is highly conserved among family groups, it is thought to be extremely low.

X-linked dominant
X-linked dominant is incorrect. X-linked dominant conditions causing liver disease include a range of porphyrias.

X-linked recessive
X-linked recessive is incorrect. Ornithine transcarbamylase deficiency is an example of an X-linked recessive cause of liver disease. Genetic.

stem: An 18-year-old woman is referred to the gastroenterology clinic for review. She is referred because of the presence of Kayser–Fleischer rings, ataxia and choreiform movements, more marked on the right than the left. You suspect Wilson’s disease. Which one of the following fits best with the diagnosis?
options: Intestinal absorption of copper is reduced
Male relatives are likely to be more severely affected
explanation:
Impaired biliary copper excretion
Wilson’s disease is an autosomal recessive disease with a prevalence of 1 in 30 000. Its clinical and pathological manifestations result from excessive accumulation of copper in many tissues, including the brain, liver, cornea and kidneys. Impaired biliary copper excretion occurs because of mutations in the ATP7B gene located on chromosome 13.

Intestinal absorption of copper is reduced
Intestinal absorption of copper is reduced is incorrect. There is no effect on intestinal copper absorption in Wilson’s.

Microcytic anaemia on blood testing
Microcytic anaemia on blood testing is incorrect. Wilson’s causes non-autoimmune-mediated haemolytic rather than microcytic anaemia.

Autoimmune haemolysis
Autoimmune haemolysis is incorrect. The haemolysis associated with Wilson’s is non-autoimmune.

Male relatives are likely to be more severely affected
Male relatives are likely to be more severely affected is incorrect. The condition is autosomal recessive, meaning that men and women are equally affected. Wilson’s.

stem: A 25-year-old man presents to the genetics counselling clinic. He has suffered from nose bleeds since the age of 17, and has a number of telangiectasias around his nose and mouth. Apparently his father suffered from the same condition and also suffered from a number of gastrointestinal haemorrhages as he increased in age. Given the likely diagnosis, which of the following correctly reflects the mode of inheritance for this condition?
explanation:
Autosomal dominant
The history given here is very suggestive of a diagnosis of hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia, a condition formerly known as Osler–Weber–Rendu syndrome. It is characterised by the formation of multiple telangiectasias and arteriovenous malformations, which can lead to significant bleeding, often with epistaxis at presentation, and in later life significant gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage, or even cerebral haemorrhage, is a possibility.While oestrogen therapy is useful in women for reducing the risk of haemorrhage, the quite obvious associated other effects limit its use in men. Laser therapy is also used to reduce bleeding from significant vascular lesions.

Autosomal recessive
Autosomal recessive is incorrect. Ataxia telangiectasia is associated as an autosomal recessive Chatdisorder. with Chromosomal non-disjunction
Chromosomal non-disjunction is incorrect. Chromosomal non-disjunction is not usually associated with the development of telangiectasia syndromes.

Sex-linked dominant
Sex-linked dominant is incorrect. X-linked bleeding disorders may be associated with GI haemorrhage, but they would not be expected to lead to the development of telangiectasias. There are however rare case reports of Xlinked disorders that lead to ocular abnormalities and the formation of telangiectasia.

Sex-linked recessive
Sex-linked recessive is incorrect. X-linked recessive bleeding disorders such as haemophilia do of course exist, but are not specifically linked with haemophilia. Genetic.

stem: A 45-year-man sustains a myocardial infarction. His serum cholesterol concentration is 9.6 mmol/l. You discover on further questioning that he has two male relatives who died of a myocardial infarction in their thirties Which of the following physical signs would most suggest a diagnosis of familial hypercholesterolaemia?
explanation:
Tendon xanthomas
Tendon xanthomas (particularly Achilles tendons and extensor tendons on the back of the hand) are specific to familial hypercholesterolaemia.

Arcus senilis
Arcus senilis is incorrect. Arcus senilis is seen in patients with familial hypercholesterolaemia, although it is also seen in individuals with an LDL cholesterol in the normal range.

Eruptive xanthomas
Eruptive xanthomas is incorrect. Eruptive xanthomas are characteristic of severe hypertriglyceridaemia

Palmar xanthomas
Palmar xanthomas is incorrect. Palmar xanthomas (typically in the palmar creases, but sometimes more extensive) are typical of familial dysbetahyperlipoproteinaemia (remnant dyslipidaemia, broad beta disease).

stem: A 22-year-old woman comes to the genetics clinic with her partner as they wish to start a family. She is completely well and takes no regular medication. Her brother is affected by hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia. Her partner’s family are unaffected by the disease. Her own father has significant problems with bruising, nose bleeds and gastrointestinal (GI) haemorrhage. What is her percentage chance of having an affected child?
explanation:
0%
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia (HHT) is inherited in an autosomal dominant pattern. As such, because the woman in question is unaffected and her partner’s family has no history of HHT, there is no chance of any offspring inheriting the disease. The most common presentations of HHT include easy bruising due to telangiectasia within the skin, nose bleeds that often present at the onset of puberty and GI bleeding beginning in the 4 th or 5 th decade. Catastrophic cerebral haemorrhage due to AV malformation is also reported. Prenatal testing is possible in affected families if the particular mutation leading to HHT has been characterised.

25%
25% is incorrect as 25% is the risk of the offspring of two carriers of a recessive disorder developing the disease.

33%
33% is incorrect as 33% is the chance of a sibling of a patient with a recessive disease not being a carrier if they are phenotypically normal.

50%
50% is incorrect as 50% is the chance of the offspring of a patient with HHT inheriting the disease.

100%
100% is incorrect as this is the risk of a patient inheriting an autosomal dominant disorder where the parent is homozygous for the disease.

stem: You see a healthy 20-year-old man in your clinic. There is no significant past medical history and he plays rugby for Saracens Rugby Club. He tells you that his brother died at the age of 7 years with cystic fibrosis (CF). What are his chances of being a carrier?
explanation:
2 in 3 (67%)
The person under assessment is disease-free; we therefore know that he must either be free of the CF gene or carry one copy of it. He therefore has a 2 in 3 chance of being a CF carrier. CF is an autosomal recessive condition (needing inheritance of both genes to cause the disease). This person is an elite sportsman thus does not have the condition (removing one of the possibilities of inheritance). The remaining options are inheriting two of the normal genes (1/3 chance) or inheriting the CF gene from mum and a normal gene from dad (1/3 chance) or inheriting the CF gene from dad and a normal gene from mum (1/3) giving a carrier state. 1/3 + 1/3 = 2/3 therefore a 2/3 or 67% chance of being a carrier.

1 in 4 (25%)
1 in 4 (25%) 1 in 4 is incorrect. This is the chance of a sibling of an affected individual also being affected with CF if we are unaware of their disease status.

1 in 3 (33%)
1 in 3 (33%) 1 in 3 is incorrect. This is the chance of a known disease-free sibling of an affected individual not being a carrier.

1 in 2 (50%)
1 in 2 (50%) 1 in 2 is incorrect. This is the chance of a sibling of an affected individual being a carrier if we are unaware of their disease status.

3 in 4 (75%)
3 in 4 (75%) 3 in 4 is incorrect.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with persistent haematuria and progressive hearing loss. His father developed renal failure and required dialysis in his early forties. Physical examination reveals bilateral sensorineural hearing loss, but no other abnormalities. What is the most likely underlying genetic defect?
explanation:
COL4A5 mutation
Mutations in the COL4A5 gene are responsible for X-linked Alport Syndrome, the most common form of the disease. Type IV collagen, encoded by this gene, is a critical structural component of the glomerular basement membrane, cochlea and lens, explaining the triad of haematuria, sensorineural hearing loss and ocular abnormalities seen in affected individuals. X-linked inheritance is supported by the patient's family history of early renal failure in a male relative, which aligns with the disease progression seen in affected males, often leading to end-stage renal disease by mid-adulthood. The presence of progressive sensorineural hearing loss, a hallmark feature of Alport Syndrome, further supports this diagnosis, as it typically develops in the second to third decade of life.

TSC2 mutation
Mutations in the TSC2 gene are associated with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), an autosomal dominant condition characterised by benign tumours in multiple organs, including the brain, skin, kidneys, heart and lungs. While renal involvement in TSC may include angiomyolipomas and cystic disease, it does not typically present with persistent haematuria as the first or predominant feature. Additionally, progressive sensorineural hearing loss is not a recognised feature of TSC, making this diagnosis unlikely. The absence of other characteristic findings, such as facial angiofibromas, cortical tubers, epilepsy or pulmonary involvement, further argues against this option.

COL4A1 mutation
Mutations in COL4A1 cause hereditary small-vessel diseases, often leading to recurrent intracerebral haemorrhages, leukoencephalopathy and porencephaly, rather than progressive renal and auditory dysfunction. While COL4A1-related disorders can affect the kidneys, they do not typically lead to isolated haematuria progressing to renal failure, distinguishing them from Alport Syndrome. Additionally, sensorineural hearing loss is not a defining feature of COL4A1 mutations, making this an unlikely explanation for the patient's symptoms. Given that the patient's family history is more suggestive of glomerular basement membrane disease with systemic manifestations, COL4A5 mutations remain the more appropriate choice.

COL4A3 mutation
Mutations in COL4A3 cause autosomal recessive Alport Syndrome (ARAS) and, less commonly, an autosomal dominant form of the disease. While ARAS presents similarly to X-linked Alport Syndrome, it often manifests earlier and with a more severe phenotype, typically requiring both parents to be carriers. The absence of consanguinity or autosomal inheritance pattern in the patient's history makes ARAS less likely. Although autosomal dominant COL4A3 mutations can cause thin basement membrane nephropathy, they generally lead to isolated haematuria without progressive renal failure or hearing loss, making X-linked Alport Syndrome (COL4A5 mutation) the most appropriate answer.

PKD1 mutation.

stem: Which underlying diagnosis could best explain his symptoms and signs?
explanation:
X-Linked adrenoleukodystrophy
This is a rare cause of adrenal insufficiency and is caused by mutations in the ABCD1 gene. This gene codes for ALD, a peroxisomal membrane transporter protein. The disorder may sometimes be misdiagnosed as AImultiple Tutor sclerosis. X-linked ALD is associated with a number of different phenotypes. The most common adult phenotype is “adrenomyeloneuropathy” which involves a combination of peripheral neuropathy and a myelopathy, with or without adrenal failure. Assay of very long chain fatty acids, which are markedly elevated, is useful in confirming the diagnosis. Lorenzo’s oil may be a useful therapy in some patients, but does not usually impact on pre-existing endocrine dysfunction.

Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis is incorrect. This case includes clear clinical and biochemical features of adrenal insufficiency. This is not a feature of multiple sclerosis.

Addison’s disease
Addison’s disease is incorrect. Addison’s disease is primary adrenal failure. Some features in this case are clearly indicative of adrenal insufficiency, but Addison’s disease alone would not be sufficient to explain the coexisting neurological symptoms and signs.

Autosomal recessive adrenoleukodystrophy
Autosomal recessive adrenoleukodystrophy is incorrect. Autosomal recessive adrenoleukodystrophy presents in neonates or young children, and is usually fatal before the age of 20 years. Clinical features include developmental delay, deafness and visual impairment.

Carotid sinus hypersensitivity
Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is incorrect. Carotid sinus hypersensitivity is a disorder of the elderly and consists of an exaggerated response to carotid sinus baroreceptor stimulation. The consequent hypotension causes transient cerebral hypoperfusion and results in dizziness or syncope. A couple attended genetic screening for an inherited condition that has been observed in the husband’s family. He has muscle weakness affecting his face and the distal muscles of his arms and legs. There is delayed relaxation when you shake his hand. More severe cases have been observed in the family, with presentation at an earlier age.

stem: A 28-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with a history of recurrent chest infections and dyspnoea on exertion. On examination, he has a short stature, pectus excavatum, and widely spaced nipples. Auscultation reveals a harsh systolic ejection murmur best heard at the left upper sternal border. What is the most likely cardiac anomaly associated with his underlying genetic condition?
explanation:
Pulmonary stenosis
Pulmonary valve stenosis is indeed common among individuals with Noonan Syndrome, manifesting through valvular obstruction from abnormal development, causing increased right ventricular pressure reflected clinically via harsh systolic ejection murmurs overlying pulmonic area (left upper sternal border). Its presentation aligns well given the patient's physical traits (eg short stature & pectus excavatum), making this diagnosis most fitting considering both the clinical picture & known syndromic associations.

Atrial septal defect
This condition involves an opening in the atrial septum that allows blood to flow between the left and right atria. While it can be seen in patients with Noonan syndrome, it is not as commonly associated as other cardiac anomalies like pulmonary stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy. The presence of an ejection murmur at the left upper sternal border also makes this less likely.

Coarctation of the aorta
This congenital condition involves narrowing of the aorta, typically presenting with hypertension in young adults or differential BP between arms and legs. It does not usually present with recurrent chest infections or dyspnoea on exertion without significant findings such as radio-femoral delay or rib notching onwith imaging. Chat Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy
Up to 30% of patients with Noonan Syndrome have either obstructive or nonobstructive hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, which could cause dyspnoea. However, its hallmark auscultatory finding is often an apical systolic murmur rather than one best heard at the left upper sternal border.

Patent ductus arteriosus
Characterised by persistent patency between descending thoracic aorta and pulmonary artery after birth, leading to continuous 'machinery' murmurs often best heard beneath clavicles rather than isolated harsh systolic murmurs; though possible in Noonan syndrome, it is less typical compared against more frequently reported defects like pulmonary stenosis.

stem: A 22-year-old man presents to his General Practitioner with concerns about his ability to make friends as a result of anxiety around social situations. On questioning, he reports that he struggled at school, and in particular, he reports difficulty with learning new tasks. There is a family history of intellectual disabilities. Physical examination reveals prominent ears, a long face and hypermobile joints. What is the most likely underlying genetic cause of his symptoms?
explanation:
Fragile X syndrome
Fragile X syndrome is caused by an expansion of the CGG triplet repeat affecting the FMR1 gene on the X chromosome. It often presents with intellectual disability, anxiety and behavioural issues, which is in keeping with the issues this patient reports. Physical characteristics such as prominent ears, a long face and hypermobile joints are classic signs associated with fragile X syndrome, making it the most likely diagnosis for this patient.

Down syndrome
Down syndrome is characterised by an extra copy of chromosome 21 (trisomy 21). It typically presents with distinct facial features such as a flat nasal bridge, epicanthal folds and Brushfield spots in the eyes. While individuals may have intellectual disabilities, they usually do not exhibit prominent ears or hypermobile joints as described in this patient’s presentation. Therefore, Down syndrome is not the most likely genetic cause.

Klinefelter syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome occurs due to an extra X chromosome (47,XXY karyotype). It commonly affects males presenting with tall stature and small testes resulting in hypogonadism and infertility rather than significant cognitive impairments or distinctive facial features noted here. The specific physical examination findings, such as prominent ears or joint hypermobility, are not typical for Klinefelter syndrome.

Turner syndrome
Turner syndrome results from monosomy or structural abnormalities involving one of the two sex chromosomes (45,X karyotype). This condition generally affects women, leading to short stature, webbed necks and primary ovarian insufficiency, but it is not usually present in men, nor does it involve notable cognitive difficulties paired with anxiety seen here. Fragile X Syndrome

Williams syndrome
Williams syndrome arises from a deletion on chromosome 7q11.23, causing unique facial features often described as "elfin", cardiovascular disease, especially supravalvular aortic stenosis alongside mild-to-moderate intellectual disability primarily impacting visuospatial skills more so than generalised learning difficulties seen here. Williams syndrome also lacks the typical physical markers like joint laxity seen in fragile X patients.

stem: A 18-year-old boy is diagnosed with haemophilia A after suffering episodes of intra-articular bleeding, and bruising to his arms and legs following relatively minor trauma. Factor VIII levels are found to be approximately 15% of normal. Which of the following family members is most likely to also suffer from a bleeding disorder?
explanation:
Mother’s brother
Haemophilia A follows an X-linked recessive mode of inheritance; hence the father cannot be the donor of his abnormal X chromosome. Equally, as it carries X-linked recessive inheritance, his mother and sister are unlikely to be affected but can suffer with minor prolongations of APTT. In contrast, his maternal uncle (mother’s brother) may well have inherited haemophilia A via an abnormal gene carried on the X chromosome.

Father
Father is incorrect. His father must have donated a Y chromosome to his son, and so cannot be the provider of the abnormal X chromosome.

Father's brother
Father's brother is incorrect. As the affected X chromosome cannot have come from the father’s side of the family.

Mother
Mother is incorrect. Although it is now recognised that women may get minor prolongations of activated partial thromboplastin time (APTT), they do not suffer from clinically significant haemophilia.

stem: A 27-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with his wife as they want to start a family. He was diagnosed with phenylketonuria as an infant, which is well controlled being on a low-protein diet. His partner does not have the disease, nor is she a carrier. What is the percentage chance that the neonate will develop phenylketonuria?
explanation:
0%
Phenylketonuria is inherited in an autosomal recessive pattern. Given the patient’s partner does not have the disease, there is no chance that his offspring can inherit two copies of the gene.

25%
The risk of a child suffering from the disease in the event that both parents are carriers is 25%.

50%
The approximate risk of a child becoming a sufferer of the disease if the partner is a carrier is 50%.

75%
The chance that a child will be either a carrier or affected in the event that both parents are carriers is 75%.

100%.

stem: A 29-year-old patient presents with weakness of his facial and distal limb muscles, which has increased over the course of the past few years. He has also been investigated in the past for gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms, including intermittent episodes of severe constipation. Examination in the clinic confirms distal limb and facial muscle weakness, and you also note delayed grip relaxation. You suspect myotonic dystrophy. Which of the following is the definitive investigation?
explanation:
Genetic testing
Specific genetic testing to demonstrate the presence of an expanded CTG repeat in the DMPK gene is the gold standard for the diagnosis of myotonic dystrophy type 1, with more than 50 repeats confirming clinical disease. GI involvement leading to significantly slowed transit time is more common versus other forms of muscular dystrophy.

CT scan
CT scan is incorrect. CT scanning to demonstrate muscle wasting is non-diagnostic in this condition.

ECG
ECG is incorrect. Although cardiac conduction defects may exist, resulting in bradycardia and degrees of heart block, this is not diagnostic of the condition.

Muscle biopsy
Muscle biopsy is incorrect. Muscle biopsy shows internalisation of nuclei in muscle cells and marked atrophy, but this is not diagnostic versus genetic testing.

Nerve conduction studies.

stem: A 22-year-old man comes to the genetics clinic for review. He has a family history of myotonic dystrophy and asks what is meant by the term ‘genetic anticipation’, which he has seen on the internet. What is genetic anticipation?
options: A genetic disease only affects children
Only the first or second offspring of a generation are affected
Successive generations present with manifestations of a genetic disease at a younger age
Symptoms are worse in childhood and then begin to resolve as age increases
explanation:
Successive generations present with manifestations of a genetic disease at a younger age
Characteristically, genetic anticipation occurs in trinucleotide repeat disorders, such as Huntington’s and myotonic dystrophy. An increase in the number of trinucleotide repeats occurs with successive generations, and symptoms usually present at a younger age each time.

A genetic disease only affects children
A genetic disease only affects children is incorrect. Although a number of genetic diseases occur only in children, that is due to high lethality and failure to survive into adulthood, rather than anticipation.

Only the first or second offspring of a generation are affected
Only the first or second offspring of a generation are affected is incorrect. This is more likely to be a reflection of random chance rather than a specific genetic disorder.

Skipping of generations occurs
Skipping of generations occurs is incorrect. Skipping of generations may occur where there is incomplete penetrance, such that an individual might carry a mutation but not necessarily display all of the manifestations of the disorder.

Symptoms are worse in childhood and then begin to resolve as age increases.

stem: A 38-year-old woman is sent as an emergency to you with an acute-onset headache and deteriorating conscious level. Her husband mentions that her brother has recently had a kidney transplant, although he is not sure why. On examination, she has a blood pressure of 188/105 mmHg; pulse is 84 and regular. Her GCS is 13 and she vomits twice. There is obvious neck stiffness. Abdominal examination reveals bilateral renal masses. What condition may be running in the family?
explanation:
Polycystic kidney disease (PKD)
The most likely diagnosis is a ruptured intracranial aneurysm. They occur in approximately 10% of individuals with autosomal dominant polycystic kidney disease (ADPKD), and approximately 50% of patients with ADPKD have end-stage renal disease by age 60 years. PKD is a relatively common genetic disorder and there are two known ADPKD genes: PKD1, accounting for about 85% of cases PKD2, accounting for about 15% of cases

Alport syndrome
Alport syndrome is incorrect. It is associated with kidney disease and deafness, coupled with non-visible haematuria, but is not associated with renal masses.

Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia
Hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia is incorrect. Cerebral arteriovenous malformations can occur in hereditary haemorrhagic telangiectasia and these may result in intracerebral bleeding, although kidney enlargement is not a feature.

Tuberous sclerosis
Tuberous sclerosis is incorrect. Renal cysts can be found in tuberous sclerosis (TS); in addition, there is a high frequency of subependymal glial nodules and cortical tubers, but these would not explain the history of sudden-onset headache, which are more likely to be associated with chronic symptoms of intracranial masses.

von Hippel–Lindau disease
von.

stem: Patients with xeroderma pigmentosum have a high risk of developing skin cancer. What kind of genetic deficiency do these patients have?
explanation:
Nucleotide excision repair
Xeroderma pigmentosum is an inherited skin disorder characterised by photosensitivity with severe sunburn in infancy, the development of numerous pigmented spots resembling freckles, larger atrophic lesions associated with telangiectasis and multiple solar keratosis. Transmitted in an autosomal recessive manner, xeroderma pigmentosum involves a defect in nucleotide excision repair (NER), leading to deficient repair of DNA damaged by UV radiation, and chromosome breakage. Individuals with this disease develop multiple malignant cutaneous neoplasms at an early age, and may suffer from severe ophthalmic and neurological abnormalities.

Base excision repair
Base excision repair is incorrect. Base excision repair is responsible primarily for removing small non-helixdistorting base lesions from the genome. Deficiencies in base excision repair are associated with an increased risk of colon cancer.

Ligase
Ligase is incorrect. Ligase facilitates the joining of DNA strands together by catalysing the formation of a phosphodiester bond. DNA ligase deficiency is thought to play a role in the development of ovarian carcinoma.

Mismatch repair
Mismatch repair is incorrect. Mismatch repair deficiencies primarily play a role in the development of oesophageal, gastric, and head and neck cancers.

Protein kinase.

stem: You are working in the Emergency Department and notice that a tall and thin 19-year-old student has attended for the second time with spontaneous pneumothorax. He displays clear signs of hyperflexibility, and on further questioning it appears he has also had problems with shoulder dislocation. He also has a reduced upper to lower body segment ratio. You suspect he may have Marfan syndrome. Which one of the following correctly describes the mutation associated with Marfan syndrome?
explanation:
Fibrillin-1 (FBN1) gene mutation
This is responsible for the structural integrity of the skeletal, ocular and cardiovascular systems. Marfan syndrome is one of the most common single-gene mutation disorders, and has a prevalence said to be between 1 in 3000 and 1 in 10 000. It carries an autosomal dominant inheritance pattern with a relatively high clinical variability. Two prominent systems of clinical classification (Berlin and Ghent) are used to characterise the disorder.

ADAMTS-2 gene mutation
ADAMTS-2 gene mutation is incorrect. An ADAMTS-2 gene mutation leads to defects in collagen fibril assembly, and so to Ehlers–Danlos syndrome.

COL3A1 gene mutation
COL3A1 gene mutation is incorrect. The COL3A1 gene contains the genetic code for production of type III collagen, and mutations lead to the development of vascular-type Ehlers–Danlos syndrome.

COL5A1 gene mutation
COL5A1 gene mutation is incorrect. COL5A1 gene mutation leads to defects in type V collagen, and is responsible for the development of the classical-type Ehlers–Danlos syndrome.

PLOD1 gene mutation.

stem: A 20-year-old man is referred for investigation of hypogonadism and infertility. He went through normal puberty and there is no significant family history. On examination he is tall with gynaecomastia and small testes. He has a normal sense of smell. Which condition would be high on your list of differential diagnoses?
explanation:
Klinefelter syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome occurs due to the presence of an additional X chromosome (XXY). It is the most common sex chromosome abnormality (1 in 600 male births) and the most common cause of male hypogonadism and infertility. Affected men tend to be tall and have an increased risk of mild intellectual impairment. Over time they also have increased risk of osteoporotic fracture due to low testosterone.

Fragile X syndrome
Fragile X syndrome is incorrect. Fragile X syndrome is associated with macroorchidism and moderate to severe learning disability. It occurs due to mutations in the FMR gene.

Kallmann syndrome
Kallmann syndrome is incorrect. Kallmann syndrome is associated with hypogonadotrophic hypogonadism and anosmia, and we are specifically told here that sense of smell is normal.

Marfan syndrome
Marfan syndrome is incorrect. Marfan’s is not associated with hypogonadism.

XYY syndrome.

stem: A 45-year-old patient who has been diagnosed with colon cancer presents with areas of hyperpigmentation around the lips, nose and within the oral cavity. He has a past history of intussusception as a child, and two episodes of gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding over the past 15 years. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Peutz–Jeghers syndrome
The lentigines in patients with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome are located primarily around the nose and mouth, on the hands and feet, and within the oral cavity. While the pigmented macules on the face may fade with age, the oral lesions persist. Hamartomas associated with Peutz–Jeghers syndrome result in intussusception in childhood, and may lead to gastrointestinal (GI) bleeding. Cumulative risk of cancer begins to rise in middle age; by age 70, risks for all, GI and pancreatic cancers are 85%, 57% and 11%, respectively.

Fanconi anaemia
Fanconi anaemia is incorrect. Although it is associated over the longer term with risk of GI cancers and acute myeloid leukaemia, the perioral pigmentation seen here is not a feature.

Neurofibromatosis type 1
Neurofibromatosis type 1 is incorrect. This is associated with axillary freckling, café au lait spots and cutaneous neurofibromas. In this case, the neurofibromas may undergo malignant transformation.

Neurofibromatosis type 2
Neurofibromatosis type 2 is incorrect. This is primarily characterised by the growth of non-cancerous tumours (acoustic neuromas and schwannomas) within the central nervous system (CNS).

Tuberous sclerosis.

stem: A 45-year-old lady is referred to you with a diagnosis of renal cell carcinoma. She tells you that she had surgery for phaeochromocytoma at the age of 25 years. A history of epilepsy is also noted. Her ultrasound scan has also noted a number of pancreatic cysts. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
von Hippel–Lindau disease
Patients with this condition are at risk of developing cerebellar, brainstem and spinal haemangioblastomas, retinal angiomas, phaeochromocytomas and paragangliomas (extra-adrenal phaeochromocytomas), renal cysts and clear cell renal cell carcinoma, pancreatic cysts and islet cell tumours, epididymal tumours and endolymphatic tumours. Renal cell carcinoma is the most common cause of death in this condition. This is an autosomal dominant cancer syndrome that is caused by mutations in the VHL gene on 3p25–p26. Diagnostic criteria: The presence of two or more haemangioblastomas (retinal or central nervous system [CNS]) The combination of a haemangioblastoma and a visceral manifestation of VHL in the absence of a family history The presence of one haemangioblastoma or visceral manifestation with a positive family history.

Familial paraganglioma
Familial paraganglioma is incorrect. This is of course associated with presence of phaeochromocytoma, but not with increased risk of renal cell carcinoma.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 1 is incorrect. This is not associated with increased risk of phaeochromocytoma or renal cell carcinoma.

Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A)
Multiple endocrine neoplasia type 2A (MEN2A) is incorrect. This is not associated with pancreatic cysts or renal cell carcinoma, and is associated with other features not seen here, such as hyperparathyroidism and medullary thyroid carcinoma.

Neurofibromatosis type 1 (NF1).

stem: A 50-year-old pub owner comes to the dermatology clinic for review. He has suffered from increasing skin fragility and a blistering rash affecting his arms, face and scalp over the past few months; he has also noticed increasing hairiness affecting his face. Routine bloods show slightly elevated transaminases. Which one of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Porphyria cutanea tarda (PCT)
Porphyria cutanea tarda is the most common of the porphyrias. It normally occurs as a sporadic condition (type I), although a rare autosomal dominant form (type II) may occur. The deficient enzyme is uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase. Cutaneous porphyrias are photosensitive disorders, which are aggravated in the summer months. PCT is most common in middle-aged men, and may be triggered by alcoholism; symptoms can be improved by reducing alcohol consumption.

Acute intermittent porphyria (AIP)
Acute intermittent porphyria is incorrect. AIP is characterised by multiple acute presentations with neuropsychiatric disturbances, hypertension and abdominal pain.

Aminolevulinic acid dehydratase porphyria (ADP)
Aminolevulinic acid dehydratase porphyria (ADP) is incorrect. ADP is a very rare form of acute intermittent porphyria, to which it has a similar presentation.

Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP)
Congenital erythropoietic porphyria (CEP) is incorrect. CEP is a cutaneous porphyria that presents in childhood with light-sensitive skin rashes.

Guttate psoriasis.

stem: A 27-year-old patient presents to the genetics clinic. She is very worried as her father died at the age of 48 from pancreatic carcinoma, and her sister has been diagnosed with a skin condition called ichthyosis. She and her partner want to start a family but wish for genetic counselling first. Which one of the following genes may be involved in a familial cancer syndrome in this patient?
explanation:
KRAS
The KRAS gene codes for a GTPase, and is an important component in many signal transduction pathways, including those driving cell growth. Around 80–90% of pancreatic adenocarcinomas have mutations demonstrated in the KRAS2 gene. Increased risk of colon cancers and leukaemias is also seen with KRAS mutation. A syndrome has been identified in which lesions consistent with ichthyosis (the scenario present here) are also seen.

NRAS
NRAS is incorrect. NRAS mutations are associated with the development of malignant melanoma, being found in up to 25% of cases.

p16
p16 is incorrect. p16 mutations are seen in around 30% of patients with chronic pancreatitis.

p53
p53 is incorrect. Although p53 mutations are associated with pancreatic cancer, they are only found in approximately 50% of pancreatic adenocarcinomas.

Rb.

stem: A 32-year-old man comes to the nephrology clinic for review. He is under investigation for arthritis of his hips and knees, where x-rays have revealed significant chondrocalcinosis. He is concerned that he may have kidney disease because he has noticed on a few occasions that his urine turns brown/black on standing. On examination his BP is 122/82, pulse is 70 and regular. The abdomen is soft and non-tender and his BMI is 25. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Alkaptonuria
This is an autosomal recessive condition of homogentisic acid oxidase deficiency, also known as ochronosis. It is associated with accelerated chondrocalcinosis and subsequent symptoms of arthritis. Homogentisic acid is oxidised in standing urine, which leads to formation of a pigmented polymer which colours urine black. Vitamin C and nitisinone are used as potential therapies for the condition.

Hyperparathyroidism
Hyperparathyroidism is incorrect. This does lead to chondrocalcinosis, although other features such as renal stones or psychiatric disturbance may be expected, and darkening of urine is not seen.

Haemochromatosis
Haemochromatosis is incorrect. This is associated with skin pigmentation, diabetes, and liver fibrosis, none of which are seen here.

Hyperuricaemia
Hyperuricaemia is incorrect. Hyperuricaemia is associated with episodes of acute monoarthritis and formation of gouty tophi.

Paroxysmal nocturnal haemoglobinuria.

stem: A 26-year-old teacher of Ashkenazi Jewish descent presents with long-standing bone pain and lethargy. On examination there is marked hepatosplenomegaly and you note that she is below expected height. Bloods reveal a normochromic normocytic anaemia, with WCC and platelets just below the lower limit of normal, and elevated transaminases. Which genetic disorder should be included in the list of differential diagnoses?
explanation:
Gaucher's disease
