Gaucher’s disease is a recessively inherited deficiency of the enzyme glucocerebrosidase, which leads to an accumulation of glucosylceramide in lysosomes. It is the most common lysosomal storage disease, and is most prevalent in the Ashkenazi Jewish population. It can be treated with enzyme replacement therapy. Type 1 disease is most common and may present in adulthood as an incidental finding. It is characterised by lack of neurological involvement. Clinical features include hepatosplenomegaly, anaemia and osteopenia. Types 2 and 3 are associated with neurological involvement and present in infancy with severe disease.

Canavan's disease
Canavan’s disease is incorrect. This presents in infancy with progressive neurological degeneration, due to a defect in aspartoacylase.

Galactosaemia
Galactosaemia is incorrect. It is not more prevalent in the Ashkenazi Jewish population. It usually presents in neonates with hypoglycaemia and acidosis, and is associated with progressive hepatosplenomegaly, cataracts and intellectual impairment.

Niemann–Pick disease type A
Niemann–Pick disease type A is incorrect. It is associated with complete deficiency of syphingomyelinase, leading to lysosomal accumulation of sphyngomyelin. This presents in infancy with central nervous system (CNS) accumulation and consequent neurological impairment, and hepatosplenomegaly.

Tay–Sachs disease.

stem: A 24-year-old, white woman presents to the Genetics Clinic with her new partner, who is also white. Her 18year-old sister has cystic fibrosis (CF) and she has been identified as a carrier of the disease; her partner has not been screened for the mutation. They want to know about the chances of having a child affected by the condition. How would you explain it to them?
options: 50% of their children will be affected, and boys will have worse disease than girls
There is a chance of less than 5% of their child being affected, whether they have a boy or a girl
It is most likely a new mutation in her sister so they do not need to worry
None of their children will be affected, but all will be carriers
They have a 25% chance of having an affected child
explanation:
There is a chance of less than 5% of their child being affected, whether they have a boy or a girl
Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder, the carrier frequency in the white population being 1 in 22. Her partner, therefore, has a 1 in 44 chance of passing on an affected gene, as we do not know his carrier status; however, she is a carrier, meaning that her chance of passing on the gene is 1 in 2. All in all this gives them a 1 in 44 x 1 in 2 chance of having an affected child, making 1 in 88 or less than 5%. There is a gene mutation on the long arm of chromosome 7, with the most common abnormality being a deletion mutation at position 508 in the amino acid sequence. This causes a defect in the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance receptor (CFTR), a chloride channel. The result is increased tenacity and viscosity of secretions leading to progressive respiratory and pancreatic failure.

50% of their children will be affected, and boys will have worse disease than girls
ChatThis withimplies a 50% of their children will be affected, and boys will have worse disease than girls is incorrect. sex-linked mode of inheritance, and cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder.

It is most likely a new mutation in her sister so they do not need to worry
It is most likely a new mutation in her sister so they do not need to worry is incorrect.

None of their children will be affected, but all will be carriers
None of their children will be affected, but all will be carriers is incorrect. Fifty per cent of their children will be carriers.

They have a 25% chance of having an affected child.

stem: A couple come to the clinic with their daughter who has Turner syndrome. They want to discuss the prognosis for their daughter with respect to both fertility and long-term health outcomes, as they have read a great deal on the internet about the disease. What condition is responsible for most of the excess mortality associated with Turner syndrome?
explanation:
Thoracic aortic aneurysm rupture
Some of the best evidence about excess mortality in women with Turner syndrome comes from the Great Britain national cohort study of 3439 women with the syndrome. In total 296 deaths occurred, with circulatory disease accounting for 41% of the excess deaths associated with Turner syndrome. Out of those circulatory deaths, the standardised mortality ratio (SMR) for aortic aneurysm was 23.6. A number of other causes of death are also more common in patients with Turner syndrome, including metabolic diseases such as diabetes mellitus and other conditions such as non-infectious colitis.

Aortic regurgitation
Aortic regurgitation is incorrect. Although both aortic regurgitation and stenosis are seen in patients with Turner’s, it accounts for a lower SMR of 17.9. The presence of significant aortic regurgitation may in itself accelerate the progression of aortic root dilatation.

Aortic stenosis
Aortic stenosis is incorrect. Although both aortic regurgitation and stenosis are seen in patients with Turner’s, it accounts for a lower SMR of 17.9. Case series suggest bicuspid aortic valve that predisposes to the development of aortic stenosis is seen in approximately 30% of women with Turner syndrome.

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is incorrect. Although the incidence of diabetes mellitus is increased in patients with Turner syndrome, it is thought to be driven by insulin resistance and is very responsive to weight loss.

Non-infectious colitis.

stem: A 32-year-old man presents to the General Practitioner with episodes of severe burning pain in his hands and feet, especially after exercise. He also reports a recent history of stroke and also experiencing frequent abdominal pain. He has a family history of renal failure. Examination reveals angiokeratomas on his trunk. What is the most likely pattern of inheritance for his condition?
explanation:
X-linked recessive
Fabry’s disease is an inherited lysosomal storage disorder caused by mutations in the GLA gene, which encodes the enzyme alpha-galactosidase A. This condition follows an X-linked recessive inheritance pattern, meaning that men are typically affected while women are usually carriers due to having two X chromosomes. In this case, our patient’s symptoms— recent history of stroke, burning pain in extremities (acroparesthesia), angiokeratomas, and gastrointestinal issues—are highly suggestive manifestations of Fabry's disease, further supported by a family history suggestive of systemic involvement like renal failure.

Autosomal dominant
Conditions with autosomal dominant inheritance typically manifest when only one copy of a mutated gene is present on one of the non-sex chromosomes (autosomes). However, Fabry’s disease does not follow this pattern; it primarily affects men due to its location on the X chromosome.

Autosomal recessive
For an autosomal recessive disorder to manifest clinically, an individual must inherit two copies of a mutated gene (one from each parent). Since Fabry's disease requires only one altered GLA gene on the single X chromosome in men to cause symptoms, this option is incorrect.

Mitochondrial
Mitochondrial inheritance involves genes passed down from mothers through mitochondrial DNA affecting both sexes equally but not following typical Mendelian patterns seen with nuclear DNA disorders. Fabry’s disease involves nuclear DNA and specifically affects more men due to its location on the X chromosome.

X-linked dominant.

stem: A young man with severe learning difficulties and congenital heart disease is referred to you for a cardiac assessment. He is accompanied by his carer who says he has a chromosome abnormality. What type of abnormality is most likely to cause such a severe phenotype?
explanation:
Unbalanced autosomal translocation
As a rule, the clinical effects of a chromosome abnormality reflect the amount of imbalance of genetic material. For example, all autosomal monosomies and most autosomal trisomies are incompatible with life, the exceptions being trisomy 13 (Patau syndrome), trisomy 18 (Edward syndrome) and trisomy 21 (Down syndrome); only the last of these carries a reasonable life expectancy.

Balanced autosomal translocation
Balanced autosomal translocation is incorrect. These translocations are not normally associated with significant morbidity.

Paracentric inversion
Paracentric inversion is incorrect. These manifest when breaks occur in one arm of a chromosome and the segment is inverted. Paracentric inversions do not involve the centromere; they are often found as an incidental finding, but occasionally may interfere with gene expression and drive a clinical disorder.

Pericentric inversion
Pericentric inversion is incorrect. These occur when an arm of a chromosome is reversed and the centromere is involved. Again, if they interfere with gene expression they may drive a clinical disorder.

Sex chromosome aneuploidy.

stem: A 17-year-old boy presented with absence of pubertal development. He had no other symptoms of note. On examination he was tall, his voice was unbroken, testes were small and there was only scanty pubic hair. His sense of smell is normal. The remainder of the examination was unremarkable. What is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation:
Klinefelter syndrome
Klinefelter syndrome affects around 1 in 1000 men and is a chromosome disorder associated with 47XXY; it is the most common chromosomal disorder associated with male hypogonadism and infertility. Phenotypic changes include poor sexual development, small or undescended testes, scanty pubic hair, gynaecomastia and infertility. Infertility, poor sexual function and gynaecomastia are the most common symptoms that lead to diagnosis. The disease involves both the loss of Leydig cells and seminiferous tubular dysgenesis. Androgen replacement restores secondary sexual characteristics, but no treatment is possible for the infertility. Confirmation of the disorder is by chromosomal analysis.

Hypopituitarism
Hypopituitarism is incorrect. The absence of other features, including signs of hypothyroidism and hypoadrenalism, makes hypopituitarism much less likely.

Kallmann syndrome
Kallmann syndrome is incorrect. Kallmann syndrome is associated with features of hypogonadism and anosmia, and is seen in both male and female patients.

Testicular feminisation
Testicular feminisation is incorrect. Testicular feminisation is associated with female external genitalia and is due to androgen resistance.

Turner syndrome.
